* **M1** is a MOSFET whose **gate** is driven by $V_{in}$ (gate current ≈ 0 → $R_{in}\rightarrow\infty$).
* The upper terminal (the one carrying the body arrow) is the **source**, tied through $R_S$ to $V_{DD}$.
* The lower terminal is the **drain**, tied through $R_D$ to ground; $V_{out}$ is taken at the drain.

**DC path:** $V_{DD}\rightarrow R_S\rightarrow M_1\rightarrow R_D\rightarrow$ GND. Because there is no bias network, the stage is **self‑biased**: the gate voltage itself sets the current through the feedback resistor.

**AC:** $V_{DD}$ is an ac ground, so $R_S$ appears from the source node to ground and $R_D$ from the output node to ground.

> **Important interpretive point:** the arrow sits on the *upper* lead, so as literally drawn this is an **n‑channel device with its source at the higher potential** – i.e. the source/drain roles are interchanged with respect to normal operation. The topology drawn (source toward the supply, drain toward ground through $R_D$) is the classic **source‑degenerated common‑source stage**, normally realized with a *p‑channel* MOSFET (whose arrow points outward). Both readings are worked out below.

---

## 2. DC (quiescent) analysis

Common to both readings:

$$V_S=V_{DD}-I_D R_S,\qquad V_{out}=V_D=I_D R_D$$

**(a) As literally drawn (n‑channel, source at top).** The effective source is the *output* node (the lower terminal is the electron‑injecting, lower‑potential terminal), so with $X\equiv V_G-V_T$:

$$I_D=\beta_n\left(V_G-I_DR_D-V_T\right)^2\;\Rightarrow\;\beta_nR_D^2I_D^2-(2\beta_nR_DX+1)I_D+\beta_nX^2=0$$

$$I_D=\frac{(2\beta_nR_DX+1)-\sqrt{1+4\beta_nR_DX}}{2\beta_nR_D^2}\qquad(\beta_n=\tfrac12\mu_nC_{ox}\tfrac WL)$$

(the smaller root is the physical one, with a valid over‑drive). Note the bias is set by **$R_D$ and $V_{in}$**; $R_S$ only drops the excess voltage. Requirements: $V_{DD}-I_DR_S>I_DR_D$, $V_{OV}=X-I_DR_D\ge0$, and $I_DR_S\le V_{DD}-V_{in}+V_T$.

**(b) p‑channel counterpart (source at $V_{DD}$).** With $X\equiv V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_T|$:

$$I_D=\beta_p\left(X-I_DR_S\right)^2\;\Rightarrow\;I_D=\frac{(2\beta_pR_SX+1)-\sqrt{1+4\beta_pR_SX}}{2\beta_pR_S^2}$$

Here the bias is set by **$R_S$** (self‑biasing). Conditions: PMOS on ($V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_T|$), and saturation $V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_T|\Rightarrow I_DR_D\le V_{in}+|V_T|$.

**Stability caveat (both cases):** the self‑bias loop has gain $g_mR$ ($R=R_D$ in (a), $R_S$ in (b)); a *unique, stable* bias requires $g_mR<1$, otherwise $I_D(V_{in})$ becomes multivalued and the stage latches to a rail.

---

## 3. Small‑signal analysis

**(a) As drawn (n‑channel, source up):** the source/drain interchange makes the output node the *effective source*, so the stage is a **common‑drain (source‑follower)** configuration. With $I=g_m(v_{in}-v_{out})+g_o(v_S'-v_{out})$, $v_S'=-IR_S$, $v_{out}=IR_D$:

$$\boxed{A_v=\frac{g_mR_D}{1+g_mR_D}}\;\approx\;+1\quad(\text{non‑inverting, }<1)$$

$$R_{out}\simeq R_D\parallel\frac{1}{g_m+g_o},\qquad R_{in}\to\infty$$

Body effect is minor (source ≈ $V_{out}$, near the substrate potential). The stage works as a **voltage buffer**, and its dc bias is referenced to ground through $R_D$.

**(b) p‑channel / standard source‑degenerated common‑source stage:** $v_S=-IR_S$, $v_{out}=IR_D$, $I=g_m(v_S-v_{in})+g_o(v_S-v_{out})$:

$$\boxed{A_v=-\frac{g_mR_D}{1+g_mR_S+g_o(R_D+R_S)}\;\approx\;-\frac{R_D}{R_S+1/g_m}}$$

(inverting). Output resistance:

$$R_{out}\simeq R_D\parallel r_o\left(1+g_mR_S\right)$$

Bulk is at $V_{DD}$, so body effect is negligible; $R_{in}\to\infty$.

---

## 4. Design comments

| | (a) n‑channel as drawn | (b) p‑channel / standard CS |
|---|---|---|
| Stage type | common‑drain (source follower) | common‑source, source‑degenerated |
| Gain | $+g_mR_D/(1+g_mR_D)$, $<1$ | $-g_mR_D/(1+g_mR_S)$ |
| $R_{out}$ | $R_D\parallel 1/g_m$ | $R_D\parallel r_o(1+g_mR_S)$ |
| Bias set by | $R_D$, $V_{in}$ | $R_S$, $V_{in}$ |
| $R_{in}$ | $\infty$ (gate) | $\infty$ (gate) |

* Source degeneration trades **gain** for **linearity** and **gain stability**: the effective transconductance becomes $g_m/(1+g_mR_S)$, so the gain depends mainly on resistor ratios rather than on $W/L$, $V_T$ or $g_m$; third‑order distortion falls sharply. Design rule for (b): $R_S\approx -R_D/A_v$ for $g_mR_S\gg1$.
* Maximum output swing is limited by the quiescent point and by the point where the device leaves saturation ($V_{out,\max}\approx V_S-V_{OV}$); the stage can be driven to $V_{out}\to0$.
* The gate draws no dc current, so the whole signal path is unidirectional; bandwidth is set by $C_{gs}+C_{gd}$ and by $C_L$ at the output.
* Since the gate voltage also sets the bias, this stage is not suited to independent biasing – a cascode or a separate bias (e.g. a second transistor) is normally added in a real design.

Here that is the **lower** terminal.

Therefore:

* the **bottom node (V_out) is the effective source**,
* the **top node (R_S–V_DD side) is the effective drain**.

**This is a common‑drain (source‑follower) stage**, drawn “upside down”: R_D is the source resistor to ground and R_S is the drain load to V_DD. (The labels R_S/R_D refer to the *marked* pins, which is why they look “reversed”.)

* The marked orientation (top = source) would require v_in > V_top + V_T ≈ V_DD + V_T, i.e. an input above the supply rail – not usable. Hence the reverse operation is the intended one.

## 3. DC analysis

Let V_G = dc value of V_in, V_O = V_out(dc), I_D = quiescent current.

$$V_O = I_D R_D,\qquad V_{top} = V_{DD} - I_D R_S$$

Effective overdrive (referenced to the *real* source = output node):

$$V_{OV} = V_G - V_O - V_T$$

In saturation: $I_D = \tfrac12 k_n V_{OV}^2$, $k_n=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)$. Combining with $V_O = I_D R_D$:

$$\frac{k_n R_D}{2}V_{OV}^2 + V_{OV} = V_G - V_T
\;\Longrightarrow\;
V_{OV}=\frac{\sqrt{1+2k_nR_D(V_G-V_T)}-1}{k_nR_D}$$

$$I_D=\tfrac12 k_nV_{OV}^2,\qquad V_O=V_G-V_T-V_{OV}$$

**Validity (saturation) conditions** – the “threshold” voltage must lie *between* the two output nodes:

$$V_O \;\le\; V_G-V_T \;\le\; V_{top}
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
I_D R_D\le V_G-V_T \quad\text{and}\quad I_D\le\frac{V_{DD}-V_G+V_T}{R_S}$$

* If $V_G-V_T < V_O$ → M1 is **cut off**, I_D = 0, V_out = 0 ⇒ **no signal transfer**. So a dc bias on V_in is essential.
* **R_S selection:** $R_S \le (V_{DD}-V_G+V_T)/I_D$. R_S does not set the current (V_in and R_D do); it supplies the current and provides drain headroom. It also caps the current: $I_{D,max}\approx(V_{DD}-V_T)/R_S$, which limits how high V_out can swing.

*Numerical illustration* (V_DD = 5 V, V_T = 1 V, k_n = 1 mA/V², V_G = 3 V, R_D = 2 kΩ):
V_OV = 1 V → I_D = 0.5 mA → V_O = 1 V; saturation needs V_top ≥ V_G−V_T = 2 V ⇒ R_S ≤ 6 kΩ; take R_S = 3 kΩ ⇒ V_top = 3.5 V ✔ (comfortably saturated).

## 4. Small‑signal analysis

V_DD is an ac ground; the model is the usual one with g_m = k_nV_OV (and r_o if desired).

**Voltage gain** (non‑inverting, ≈ unity):

$$A_v=\frac{v_o}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_mR_D}{1+g_mR_D}\;\xrightarrow[g_mR_D\gg1]{}\;+1$$

so V_out is a level‑shifted replica of V_in: $v_o \approx v_{in}$ shifted down by (V_T + V_OV).

With finite r_o and drain resistor:

$$A_v=\frac{\alpha g_mR_D}{1+\alpha R_D\left(g_m+\frac1{r_o}\right)},\qquad \alpha=\frac{r_o}{r_o+R_S}\approx1$$

Note that **R_S does not affect the gain** (it only affects bias, headroom and swing limit).

**Other ac parameters**

* $R_{in}\approx\infty$ (gate); at high frequency C_gs, C_gd load the input, but Miller multiplication is negligible because A_v ≈ 1.
* $R_{out}=\left[\frac1{R_D}+\alpha\!\left(g_m+\frac1{r_o}\right)\right]^{-1}\approx\frac1{g_m}\parallel R_D$ (low impedance output).
* Dominant pole at the output node: $f_p\approx\frac{1}{2\pi R_{out}C_L}$.

## 5. What the circuit does

| Property | Result |
|---|---|
| Configuration | Common‑drain (source follower), NMOS run in reverse |
| Gain | $A_v=+g_mR_D/(1+g_mR_D)\approx+1$ (non‑inverting buffer) |
| R_in | ∞ |
| R_out | ≈ 1/g_m ∥ R_D |
| Bias | set by V_in(dc) and R_D: $V_O=V_{in}-V_T-V_{OV}$ |
| Output range | low end ≈ 0 V; high end limited by saturation ($V_{top}\ge V_G-V_T$, i.e. by R_S) |
| Use | level shifter / voltage buffer, high Z_in, low Z_out |

## 6. Practical caveats

* **Body effect / substrate:** the arrow ties the body to the *marked* source (the top node, near V_DD). With the device reversed, the body–source junction becomes forward biased unless a body‑isolated device is used (e.g. PMOS in an n‑well, SOI, or a discrete MOSFET with the body handled separately). Textbook analyses ignore this.
* **Reverse operation** slightly degrades on‑resistance and speed compared with normal source/drain assignment.
* The dc level of V_in is not optional – without it the transistor is off and V_out sits at 0 V.

# Analysis of the Circuit

## 1. Reading the schematic

The arrow on the upper transistor terminal identifies that terminal as the **source** of $M_1$; the lower terminal (where $V_{out}$ is taken) is the **drain**, and the gate is driven by $V_{in}$.

| Node | Connection |
|---|---|
| Gate | $V_{in}$ (input) |
| Source | through $R_S$ to $V_{DD}$ (source degeneration) |
| Drain | $V_{out}$, loaded by $R_D$ to ground |

Because the source is the *high‑potential* terminal and the drain is the *low‑potential* terminal, $M_1$ must be a **PMOS** for the stage to be biasable (with $V_G \approx 0$, an N‑channel device with its source at the $V_{DD}$ side could never be on).

**Topology:** a **common‑source (common‑emitter) amplifier with source degeneration**, using a PMOS. Note that $V_{DD}$ is an **AC ground**, so both $R_S$ and $R_D$ appear as resistances to ground in the small‑signal model.

**Operation:** a positive change in $V_{in}$ reduces $V_{SG}$, reduces $|I_D|$, and therefore *lowers* $V_{out}$ → the stage is **inverting**.

---

## 2. DC bias analysis

The dc current path is $V_{DD}\rightarrow R_S\rightarrow M_1\rightarrow R_D\rightarrow$ ground:

$$V_S = V_{DD}-I_D R_S,\qquad V_D = I_D R_D,\qquad V_{SG}=V_S-V_G$$

With $K=\tfrac12\mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)$ and in saturation:

$$I_D = K\left(V_{SG}-|V_T|\right)^2 = K V_{OV}^2$$

Solving the bias loop (with $V_G$ = dc level of $V_{in}$), letting $x=V_{OV}$:

$$K R_S x^2 + x - (V_{DD}-V_G-|V_T|)=0 \;\Rightarrow\; x=\frac{-1+\sqrt{1+4KR_S(V_{DD}-V_G-|V_T|)}}{2KR_S}$$

$$I_D=Kx^2,\qquad V_{out,DC}=I_D R_D,\qquad V_S=V_{DD}-I_D R_S$$

**Saturation test:** $V_{SD}\ge V_{OV}$, which reduces to the simple and often overlooked condition

$$\boxed{V_D = I_D R_D \;\le\; V_G+|V_T|}$$

So $R_D$ must be kept small enough that the drop across it does not exceed $V_G+|V_T|$.

**Output range:** $V_{out}$ swings from $\approx 0$ (device off) up to $V_G+|V_T|$ (triode limit). The available swing is therefore governed by the **gate bias**; biasing the gate at $V_G>0$ (rather than at 0 V) is what makes a useful swing possible.

---

## 3. Small‑signal analysis

Small‑signal parameters: $g_m = 2I_D/V_{OV}$, $r_o = 1/(\lambda I_D)$; replace $V_{DD}$ by an ac ground.

**Source node (KCL):**

$$\frac{v_s}{R_S}=g_m(v_{in}-v_s)\;\Rightarrow\;v_{gs}=v_{gs}=v_{in}-v_s=\frac{v_{in}}{1+g_mR_S}$$

The source "follows" the gate through the degeneration feedback, so only $v_{in}/(1+g_mR_S)$ appears across $g_m$.

**Drain node (KCL):**

$$v_{out} = -g_m v_{gs}\,(R_D\|r_o)$$

$$\boxed{A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=-\frac{g_m\,(R_D\|r_o)}{1+g_mR_S}\approx-\frac{g_mR_D}{1+g_mR_S}}$$

* Magnitude is reduced by the factor $(1+g_mR_S)$ compared with a plain common‑source stage ($R_S=0$).
* The stage is **inverting**; $\lvert A_v\rvert \le g_m(R_D\|r_o)$ and $\lvert A_v\rvert \to 0$ as $R_S\to\infty$.
* The degeneration also makes the gain nearly independent of $g_m$ (i.e., less sensitive to device variations and temperature).

**Input resistance:** $R_{in}=\infty$ (MOSFET gate; only the bias network would load it).

**Output resistance** (input set to ac ground, source resistor not to ac ground):

$$R_{out}=R_D\;\Big\|\;\big[r_o+R_S+g_m r_oR_S\big]\approx R_D\,\|\,r_o(1+g_mR_S)$$

---

## 4. Results at a glance

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| Type | PMOS common‑source with source degeneration |
| Voltage gain | $A_v=-\dfrac{g_m(R_D\|r_o)}{1+g_mR_S}$ (inverting) |
| Input resistance | $\infty$ |
| Output resistance | $R_D\|[r_o(1+g_mR_S)+R_S]\approx R_D\|r_o(1+g_mR_S)$ |
| Bias constraint (saturation) | $I_D R_D\le V_G+|V_T|$ |
| Output swing | $0 \le V_{out}\le V_G+|V_T|$ |
| Bandwidth | Broad‑band; no compensation capacitor, limited only by $C_{gs},C_{gd},C_{db}$ and the drain node capacitance |

---

## 5. Observations

1. **Source degeneration as local feedback:** $R_S$ makes the source node track the gate, stabilising $I_D$ against $g_m$ variations (good linearity, but the price is gain).
2. **Body effect:** for a discrete PMOS with the body tied to the source, $V_{SB}=0$ and $V_T$ is constant. In an IC with the n‑well tied to $V_{DD}$, $V_{SB}=-I_DR_S$, so $|V_T|$ grows with current; this adds a second‑order term ($g_{mb}$) that slightly reduces the gain.
3. **Headroom:** the drain load $R_D$ sits at the *output* side of a PMOS, so the usable output range is limited to $V_G+|V_T|$; the gain and swing must be traded against $R_D$.
4. **No Miller multiplication:** the gate is the input and the drain is the output, so this stage adds essentially no input capacitance.

*Symbol note:* if the arrow in your original figure is meant as an **N‑channel** source arrow (pointing into the channel), then the upper terminal is the drain and the lower one the source, and the same node structure becomes a **source follower** (common‑drain): $A_v=+g_mR_D/(1+g_mR_D)\approx1$ (non‑inverting), $R_{in}=\infty$, $R_{out}\approx (1/g_m)\|R_D$, with the source resistor now the one going to ground. The identification of $R_S$ (top) and $R_D$ (bottom) in the figure, however, is consistent with the common‑source interpretation above.

## 1. Circuit identification

The device symbol indicates a **p-channel MOSFET (pMOS)**. Its source is the upper terminal and its drain is the lower terminal. Therefore, the dc current path is

\[
V_{DD}\rightarrow R_S\rightarrow M_1\rightarrow R_D\rightarrow \text{ground}.
\]

This is a **source-degenerated common-source pMOS stage**:

- \(R_S\): source degeneration; it also establishes the dc source voltage.
- \(R_D\): drain load to ground.
- Output: taken at the drain, \(V_{\text{out}}=V_D\).
- Input: applied to the MOS gate.

Because \(V_{DD}\) is an ac ground, \(R_S\) is seen by the transistor as a source resistor to ground during small-signal analysis.

---

## 2. DC operating point

Let

- \(V_{TP}=|V_{TH,p}|\),
- \(\beta_p=\mu_p C_{\text{ox}}(W/L)\),
- \(I_Q\) be the dc drain current.

The dc node voltages are

\[
V_S=V_{DD}-I_Q R_S,
\]

\[
V_{\text{out}}=V_D=I_QR_D,
\]

and

\[
V_{SG}=V_S-V_{\text{in}}
      =V_{DD}-I_QR_S-V_{\text{in}}.
\]

If \(M_1\) operates in saturation and channel-length modulation is neglected,

\[
I_Q=\frac{\beta_p}{2}\left(V_{SG}-V_{TP}\right)^2
=\frac{\beta_p}{2}
\left(V_{DD}-V_{\text{in}}-I_QR_S-V_{TP}\right)^2.
\]

For \(\lambda=0\), define

\[
A=V_{DD}-V_{\text{in}}-V_{TP}.
\]

The positive solution is

\[
I_Q=
\left[
\frac{
\sqrt{2/\beta_p+4R_SA}-\sqrt{2/\beta_p}
}{2R_S}
\right]^2,
\qquad
V_{\text{out},Q}=I_QR_D.
\]

If \(R_S=0\), this reduces to

\[
I_Q=\frac{\beta_p}{2}
\left(V_{DD}-V_{\text{in}}-V_{TP}\right)^2.
\]

### Region checks

The source-to-drain voltage is

\[
V_{SD}=V_{DD}-I_Q(R_S+R_D).
\]

- **Cutoff:** \(V_{SG}\le V_{TP}\)
- **Saturation:** \(V_{SG}>V_{TP}\) and \(V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-V_{TP}\)
- **Triode:** \(V_{SG}>V_{TP}\) and \(0<V_{SD}<V_{SG}-V_{TP}\)

In triode,

\[
I_Q=\beta_p\left[(V_{SG}-V_{TP})V_{SD}-\frac{V_{SD}^2}{2}\right].
\]

There is no separate bias network in the drawing, so \(V_{\text{in}}\) must include the required dc bias voltage.

---

## 3. Small-signal voltage gain

At midband, \(V_{DD}\) is ac ground. Define positive magnitudes

\[
g_m=\beta_p(V_{SG,Q}-V_{TP}),\qquad
g_o=\frac{1}{r_o}\simeq \lambda I_Q.
\]

With no external load, the low-frequency gain is

\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_{\text{in}}}
=
-\frac{g_mR_D}
{1+g_mR_S+g_o(R_S+R_D)}
}
\]

Ignoring \(r_o\),

\[
\boxed{
A_v\simeq-\frac{g_mR_D}{1+g_mR_S}
}
\]

Thus the stage is **inverting**:

\[
V_{\text{in}}\uparrow
\;\Rightarrow\;
V_{SG}\downarrow
\;\Rightarrow\;
I_D\downarrow
\;\Rightarrow\;
V_{\text{out}}\downarrow.
\]

The source degeneration reduces the effective transconductance to approximately

\[
g_{m,\text{eff}}=\frac{g_m}{1+g_mR_S}.
\]

---

## 4. Input and output resistances

Because the MOS gate draws essentially no current,

\[
\boxed{R_{\text{in}}\rightarrow\infty}
\]

apart from gate leakage and capacitive effects.

With the input set to ac ground, the resistance looking into the drain is approximately

\[
r_{\text{out,stage}}=r_o+R_S(1+g_mr_o).
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{out}}
=
R_D\parallel
\left[r_o+R_S(1+g_mr_o)\right]
}
\]

and for \(\lambda=0\), \(R_{\text{out}}\approx R_D\).

---

## 5. Large-signal behavior

The transfer characteristic is

\[
V_{\text{out}}(V_{\text{in}})
=
R_D I_D(V_{\text{in}}),
\]

and it decreases as \(V_{\text{in}}\) increases.

- At cutoff, \(I_D=0\), so \(V_{\text{out}}=0\).
- The maximum possible current is limited by the two resistors:

\[
I_D\le \frac{V_{DD}}{R_S+R_D},
\]

hence

\[
V_{\text{out}}\le
\frac{V_{DD}R_D}{R_S+R_D}.
\]

The practical maximum may be lower depending on the available gate-source overdrive and whether the transistor enters triode.

## Summary

This is a **source-degenerated, common-source pMOS amplifier**. Its key results are

\[
A_v\simeq-\frac{g_mR_D}{1+g_mR_S},
\qquad
R_{\text{in}}\text{ is very high},
\]

\[
R_{\text{out}}
\simeq
R_D\parallel\left[r_o+R_S(1+g_mr_o)\right].
\]

A numerical bias point and gain require \(V_{DD}\), \(R_S\), \(R_D\), \(V_{\text{in},Q}\), \(V_{TP}\), \(\beta_p\), and \(\lambda\).

## 1. Circuit identification

The upper, arrowed terminal is the **source**, and the lower terminal is the **drain**. Since the source is connected toward \(V_{DD}\) and the drain toward ground through \(R_D\), \(M_1\) is most reasonably interpreted as a **p-channel MOSFET**.

This is a **common-source amplifier with source degeneration**:

- Input: gate, \(v_{in}\)
- Output: drain, \(v_{out}\)
- \(R_S\): source-bias and degeneration resistor
- \(R_D\): drain load
- \(V_{DD}\) is AC ground

It is not a common-gate stage; a common-gate amplifier would have the signal applied to the source and the gate held at AC ground.

A DC gate bias \(V_{G,Q}\) is also required. If \(V_{in}\) is purely a zero-mean AC signal, a separate gate-bias network is missing from the drawing.

---

## 2. DC bias

The dc current path is

\[
V_{DD}\rightarrow R_S\rightarrow M_1\rightarrow R_D\rightarrow \text{ground}.
\]

Let

\[
V_T=|V_{TH,p}|,\qquad
V_{OV}=V_{SG}-V_T,
\qquad
\beta_p=\frac{1}{2}\mu_p C_{ox}\frac WL .
\]

Assuming saturation and neglecting channel-length modulation,

\[
I_D=\beta_p V_{OV}^2.
\]

The resistor voltages are

\[
V_S=V_{DD}-I_D R_S,
\qquad
V_D=I_D R_D.
\]

Hence, with gate dc voltage \(V_{G,Q}\),

\[
V_{OV}=V_{DD}-V_{G,Q}-V_T-I_D R_S,
\]

and the bias current satisfies

\[
\boxed{
I_{DQ}=
\beta_p
\left(
V_{DD}-V_{G,Q}-V_T-I_{DQ}R_S
\right)^2
}
\]

which can be solved numerically or analytically. Defining

\[
A=V_{DD}-V_{G,Q}-V_T,
\]

the positive solution is

\[
\sqrt{I_{DQ}}
=
\frac{\sqrt{1+4\beta_pR_SA}-1}
     {2R_S\sqrt{\beta_p}}.
\]

The pMOS must satisfy the saturation condition

\[
\boxed{V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-V_T}
\]

or, equivalently,

\[
V_D\le V_G+V_T.
\]

If this condition is violated, \(M_1\) is in the triode region.

---

## 3. Small-signal voltage gain

Define

\[
g_m=2\beta_pV_{OV}=\frac{2I_D}{V_{OV}},
\qquad
r_o=\frac{1}{\lambda I_D}.
\]

Because \(V_{DD}\) is AC ground, \(R_S\) appears from the source to AC ground. Ignoring \(r_o\), the source follows the gate partially:

\[
v_s=\frac{g_mR_S}{1+g_mR_S}v_{in},
\]

so that

\[
v_{gs}=v_{in}-v_s
=\frac{v_{in}}{1+g_mR_S}.
\]

For a pMOS, an increase in gate voltage reduces the source-to-gate voltage and therefore reduces the drain current. Consequently, the stage is inverting:

\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
\simeq
-\frac{g_mR_D}{1+g_mR_S}
}
\]

when \(r_o\) is neglected.

With finite \(r_o\) included, nodal analysis gives

\[
\boxed{
A_v=
-\frac{g_mR_Dr_o}
{r_o(1+g_mR_S)+R_S+R_D}
}
\]

which reduces to the preceding expression for \(r_o\to\infty\).

Useful limiting cases are

\[
R_S=0:
\qquad
A_v=-g_m(R_D\parallel r_o),
\]

and for strong degeneration \(g_mR_S\gg1\),

\[
A_v\approx-\frac{R_D}{R_S}.
\]

---

## 4. Input and output resistance

Because the MOSFET gate draws essentially no current,

\[
\boxed{R_{in}\rightarrow\infty}
\]

except for gate leakage and capacitances.

Looking back into the drain with the gate at AC ground, the amplifier output resistance is approximately

\[
R_{out,M1}=r_o+R_S(1+g_mr_o).
\]

Including \(R_D\),

\[
\boxed{
R_{out}
=
R_D\parallel
\left[r_o+R_S(1+g_mr_o)\right]
}
\]

Thus source degeneration increases output resistance while reducing gain and improving linearity.

---

## 5. Main conclusions

- The stage is a **p-channel common-source amplifier with source degeneration**.
- It provides a voltage gain that is negative, i.e. a \(180^\circ\) phase reversal.
- \(R_S\) establishes the dc bias and provides negative feedback.
- The input impedance is very high.
- The output impedance is increased by \(R_S\).
- The source degeneration reduces gain but improves gain stability and linearity.
- A gate dc-bias network must be added or included in \(V_{in}\).

If \(M_1\) was intended to be an **n-channel** MOSFET, the source/drain polarities in the drawing are reversed: an nMOS source should normally be connected toward ground through \(R_S\), while its drain should be connected toward \(V_{DD}\) through \(R_D\).

The source arrow and the \(R_S/R_D\) labeling indicate that \(M_1\) is a **p-channel MOSFET**. The stage is a **common-source amplifier with source degeneration**:

- Input: gate voltage \(V_{\text{in}}\)
- Output: drain voltage \(V_{\text{out}}\)
- \(R_S\): source-degeneration resistor
- \(R_D\): drain load resistor
- \(V_{DD}\): supply
- \(R_S\) is not bypassed, so it provides degeneration over the full signal bandwidth.

Because no component values are given, the results can only be stated symbolically.

---

## 2. DC bias

Let the quiescent gate voltage be

\[
V_{GQ}\equiv V_{\text{in,Q}},
\]

and let the magnitude of the PMOS threshold voltage be \(|V_{TP}|\).

Since the MOSFET gate draws negligible current, the DC current is

\[
I_{DQ}=I_{S}=I_D.
\]

Therefore,

\[
V_{SQ}=V_{DD}-I_{DQ}R_S,
\]

\[
V_{DQ}=V_{out,Q}=I_{DQ}R_D,
\]

and the source-to-gate voltage is

\[
V_{SGQ}=V_{DD}-I_{DQ}R_S-V_{GQ}.
\]

Assuming saturation and defining

\[
k_p=\mu_p C_{\text{ox}}\frac WL,
\]

the PMOS current is

\[
I_{DQ}=\frac{k_p}{2}
\left(V_{SGQ}-|V_{TP}|\right)^2.
\]

Thus \(I_{DQ}\) satisfies

\[
\boxed{
I_{DQ}=
\frac{k_p}{2}
\left[
V_{DD}-V_{GQ}-|V_{TP}|-I_{DQ}R_S
\right]^2
}
\]

and the quiescent output is

\[
\boxed{V_{\text{out},Q}=I_{DQ}R_D}.
\]

For \(R_S>0\), define

\[
\Delta=V_{DD}-V_{GQ}-|V_{TP}|.
\]

An explicit saturation-current solution is

\[
I_{DQ}=
\left[
\frac{
\sqrt{\frac{2}{k_p}+4R_S\Delta}
-\sqrt{\frac{2}{k_p}}
}{2R_S}
\right]^2.
\]

### Saturation requirement

The PMOS must satisfy

\[
V_{SQ}-V_{DQ}\geq V_{SGQ}-|V_{TP}|,
\]

or equivalently,

\[
\boxed{I_{DQ}R_D\leq V_{GQ}+|V_{TP}|}.
\]

Also, the overdrive voltage

\[
V_{OV}=V_{SGQ}-|V_{TP}|
\]

must be positive.

---

For AC analysis, \(V_{DD}\) is ground, so \(R_S\) connects the source to AC ground. Neglecting \(r_o\), define

\[

### 1. Circuit Identification & Topology

  * The arrow on the upper terminal points *into* the transistor (toward the gate), which is the standard symbol for a PMOS.
  * The source ($S$) is connected to the higher potential (towards $V_{DD}$ through $R_S$), and the drain ($D$) is connected to the lower potential (towards ground through $R_D$).
* **Terminals**:
  * **Gate (G)**: Connected to the input voltage $V_{\text{in}}$.
  * **Source (S)**: Connected to $V_{DD}$ via resistor $R_S$. Since $V_{DD}$ is an AC ground, $R_S$ acts as a **source degeneration resistor**.
  * **Drain (D)**: Connected to ground via resistor $R_D$, and the output $V_{\text{out}}$ is taken from this node.
* **Configuration**: Because the input is at the gate and the output is at the drain, this is a **Common-Source (CS) amplifier**.

---

### 2. DC Analysis (Biasing)
Let the DC input voltage be $V_G = V_{\text{in, DC}}$. Assuming the transistor operates in the **saturation region**:

1. The DC current $I_D$ flowing from $V_{DD}$ to ground is:
   $$I_D = \frac{V_{DD} - V_S}{R_S} = \frac{V_D}{R_D}$$

2. The source-gate voltage is $V_{SG} = V_S - V_G$. In saturation, the current is:
   $$I_D = \frac{1}{2} \mu_p C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} (V_{SG} - |V_{THP}|)^2 (1 + \lambda V_{SD})$$
   where $V_{SD} = V_S - V_D$, and $\lambda$ is the channel-length modulation parameter.

By equating these equations, we can solve for the quiescent (DC) operating point: $V_S$, $V_D$, and $I_D$. For the transistor to remain in saturation, the condition $V_{SD} \ge V_{SG} - |V_{THP}|$ must hold.

---

### 3. Small-Signal Analysis
For AC analysis, we replace $V_{DD}$ with an **AC ground** and replace $M_1$ with its small-signal hybrid-$\pi$ model, characterized by:
* **Transconductance**: $g_m = \mu_p C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} (V_{SG} - |V_{THP}|) = \sqrt{2 \mu_p C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} I_D}$
* **Output resistance**: $r_o = \frac{1}{\lambda I_D}$

#### A. Voltage Gain ($A_v = \frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_{\text{in}}}$)
Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) at the source node ($v_s$) and the drain node ($v_{\text{out}}$):

* **At the source node ($v_s$):**
  $$\frac{v_s}{R_S} = g_m (v_{\text{in}} - v_s) + \frac{v_s - v_{\text{out}}}{r_o}$$

* **At the drain node ($v_{\text{out}}$):**
  $$\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{R_D} + g_m (v_{\text{in}} - v_s) + \frac{v_{\text{out}} - v_s}{r_o} = 0$$

Solving this system of linear equations yields the **exact voltage gain**:
$$A_v = \frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_{\text{in}}} = -\frac{g_m R_D r_o}{R_S + R_D + r_o + g_m R_S R_D} = -\frac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S + \frac{R_S + R_D}{r_o}}$$

* **Simplified Case (neglecting channel-length modulation, $r_o \to \infty$):**
  $$A_v = -\frac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S}$$

* **Strong Degeneration Limit ($g_m R_S \gg 1$):**
  $$A_v \approx -\frac{R_D}{R_S}$$
  In this regime, the gain is determined solely by the ratio of the resistors, making the amplifier highly linear and insensitive to variations in transistor parameters (like $g_m$ due to temperature or process variations).

#### B. Output Impedance ($R_{\text{out}}$)
Looking into the output node (drain) with the input $v_{\text{in}}$ set to $0$:
* The resistance looking into the drain of a source-degenerated transistor is:
  $$R_{\text{drain}} = r_o(1 + g_m R_S) + R_S$$
* The total output impedance is the parallel combination with $R_D$:
  $$R_{\text{out}} = R_D \parallel \left[ r_o(1 + g_m R_S) + R_S \right]$$
  *(If $r_o \to \infty$, then $R_{\text{out}} \approx R_D$.)*

#### C. Input Impedance ($R_{\text{in}}$)
At low frequencies, the gate of the MOSFET is insulated and draws no current:
$$R_{\text{in}} = \infty$$

1. **Inverting Amplifier**: The gain $A_v$ is negative, meaning the output signal is **$180^\circ$ out of phase** with the input.
2. **Role of $R_S$ (Source Degeneration)**:

   * Significantly improves **linearity** (reduces harmonic distortion).

3. **Role of $R_D$**: Acts as the load resistor that converts the transistor's drain current into the output voltage ($v_{\text{out}} = -i_d R_D$).

Saturation condition for the PMOS:

$$V_{SD} \ge V_{SG}-|V_{THp}| \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; V_{out} \le V_{in} + |V_{THp}|$$

So the input must be low enough (relative to V_DD) to keep V_SG > |V_THp|, and the output must stay below V_in + |V_THp| to avoid triode.

---

# 2. Small-Signal Analysis

V_DD is an AC ground, so R_S hangs from the source to ground and R_D from the drain to ground. The gate draws no current (Z_in ≈ ∞ at low frequency).

**Source node (KCL):**
$$v_s = \frac{g_m R_S}{1+g_m R_S}\,v_{in}$$
(the source "follows" the gate — this is the degeneration action)

**Output node:** the current pushed from source to drain is $g_m(v_s - v_{in})$, giving

$$\boxed{A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = -\frac{g_m R_D}{1+g_m R_S}} \quad (r_o \to \infty)$$

Including r_o:

$$A_v = -\frac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S + \dfrac{R_S+R_D}{r_o}} = -\frac{g_m R_D\,(r_o+R_S)}{r_o+R_S+R_D+g_m r_o R_S}$$

**Body effect:** the PMOS body is tied to V_DD (AC ground) while the source moves, so g_mb acts. Replacing g_m → g_m + g_mb in the denominator:

$$A_v \approx -\frac{g_m R_D}{1+(g_m+g_{mb})R_S}$$

**Key limit — if g_m R_S ≫ 1:**
$$A_v \approx -\frac{R_D}{R_S}\cdot\frac{1}{1+\eta}, \qquad \eta = g_{mb}/g_m$$
The gain is then set almost entirely by the **resistor ratio**, insensitive to g_m, temperature, and process — the main benefit of degeneration.

**Other impedances:**
- Input resistance: $R_{in} \approx \infty$ (gate)
- Effective transconductance: $G_m = \dfrac{g_m}{1+g_m R_S} \approx \dfrac{1}{R_S}$
- Output resistance: $R_{out} = R_D \parallel \left[r_o(1+g_m R_S) + R_S\right]$

The stage is **inverting**: raising V_in lowers V_SG, reduces I_D, and pulls V_out down.

---

# 3. Role of R_S (Source Degeneration)

| Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|
| Stabilizes I_D against V_TH/temperature/process shifts | Reduced gain (≈ −R_D/R_S instead of −g_m R_D) |
| Linearizes the stage (larger linear input range, less distortion) | Extra thermal noise from R_S |
| Makes gain a precise resistor ratio (PVT-insensitive) | Voltage headroom lost: I_D·R_S drop |
| Reduces the effect of g_m variation | Extra pole at the source node (C_gs with R_S) |

---

# 4. Large-Signal Behavior / Swing

- **V_in near V_DD:** V_SG < |V_THp|, M₁ off, I_D ≈ 0 → **V_out ≈ 0**
- **V_in decreasing:** M₁ turns on in saturation, V_out = I_D R_D rises with slope ≈ −R_D/R_S
- **V_in very low:** M₁ enters triode; V_out saturates near $V_{DD}\frac{R_D}{R_D+R_S+R_{on}}$

So the output swing is roughly 0 → (V_in + |V_THp|), limited at the top by the saturation condition and by triode action.

---

# 5. Summary

This is a **PMOS common-source stage with source degeneration**, i.e., a voltage-to-current converter (G_m ≈ 1/R_S) driving the load resistor R_D:

$$v_{out} = -\,G_m R_D\, v_{in}, \qquad G_m \approx \frac{g_m}{1+(g_m+g_{mb})R_S}$$

It provides a well-defined, linear, inverting gain of about −R_D/R_S (with body effect, −R_D/[(1+η)R_S]), very high input impedance, and a stable bias point — at the expense of gain, noise, and voltage headroom. It is the PMOS counterpart of the standard NMOS CS stage and is commonly used for PMOS-input amplifier stages (input referenced toward V_DD) and in discrete MOS amplifier designs.

   V_S = V_{DD} - I_D R_S

2. **Gate-source voltage**:

3. **MOSFET in saturation** (assuming $ V_{GS} > V_{th} $ and $ V_{DS} > V_{GS} - V_{th} $):
   $$
   I_D = \frac{1}{2} k_n (V_{GS} - V_{th})^2
   $$
   where $ k_n = \mu_n C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} $ is the transistor transconductance parameter, and $ V_{th} $ is the threshold voltage.

Substituting $ V_{GS} $ into the saturation equation:
$$
I_D = \frac{1}{2} k_n \left( V_{\text{in}} - V_{DD} + I_D R_S - V_{th} \right)^2
$$
This is a **quadratic equation** in $ I_D $. Solving it (numerically or graphically) gives the **DC drain current** $ I_D $, which determines:
- $ V_S = V_{DD} - I_D R_S $
- $ V_D = I_D R_D $ (since $ R_D $ connects the drain to ground)

> **Key Insight**: The presence of $ R_S $ introduces **negative feedback**, stabilizing the bias point against variations in $ V_{th} $ or $ k_n $.

---

---

### **🔹 Small-Signal Analysis (AC Response)**
For **AC signals**, $ V_{DD} $ is treated as **AC ground**, so $ R_S $ connects the source to AC ground. The small-signal model is:

- **Input**: $ v_{\text{in}} $ (AC component of $ V_{\text{in}} $)

From the small-signal model:
$$
i_d = g_m (v_{\text{in}} - v_s) = g_m (v_{\text{in}} + i_d R_S)

$$
v_{\text{out}} = -i_d R_D = -\frac{g_m R_D v_{\text{in}}}{1 - g_m R_S} = \frac{g_m R_D v_{\text{in}}}{g_m R_S - 1}
$$

$$
A_v = \frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_{\text{in}}} = \frac{g_m R_D}{g_m R_S - 1}

$$
A_v \approx \frac{R_D}{R_S}

| **Frequency Response** | Limited by parasitic capacitances (e.g., $ C_{GS} $, $ C_{GD} $)     |
| **Bias Stability**     | Improved due to negative feedback from $ R_S $                      |

---

---

### **🔹 Practical Considerations**
1. **Biasing**:
   - $ V_{\text{in}} $ must be set such that $ V_{GS} > V_{th} $ (for nMOS) to ensure the transistor is in **saturation**.
   - Example: If $ V_{DD} = 5\,\text{V} $, $ R_S = 1\,\text{k}\Omega $, $ R_D = 2\,\text{k}\Omega $, and $ V_{th} = 1\,\text{V} $, choose $ V_{\text{in}} $ to satisfy $ V_{GS} > 1\,\text{V} $.

3. **Transistor Type**:
   - If $ M_1 $ is a **pMOS**, the analysis is similar, but the **sign of the gain flips** (non-inverting amplifier). The condition for conduction becomes $ V_{SG} > |V_{th}| $.

---

---

### **🔹 Summary**
- **Circuit Type**: Common-source amplifier with **source degeneration**.
- **DC Behavior**: Bias point determined by $ V_{DD} $, $ R_S $, $ R_D $, and MOSFET parameters.
- **AC Behavior**: Voltage gain $ A_v \approx R_D / R_S $ (for $ g_m R_S \gg 1 $), with high input resistance and moderate output resistance.

### **Circuit Analysis: Common-Source Amplifier with Source Degeneration**

The given circuit is a **common-source MOSFET amplifier with source degeneration**, implemented using an **n-channel MOSFET (M₁)**. Below is a structured analysis covering **DC biasing**, **small-signal behavior**, and **key performance metrics**.

---

---

## **🔹 1. Circuit Configuration & Component Roles**
- **M₁**: n-channel MOSFET (source degeneration via $ R_S $).
- **$ V_{DD} $**: Supply voltage.
- **$ R_D $**: Drain resistor (load for the amplifier).
- **$ R_S $**: Source resistor (introduces *source degeneration*).
- **$ V_{in} $**: Input signal at the gate.
- **$ V_{out} $**: Output signal at the drain (between $ R_D $ and M₁).

> **Note**: The diagram shows $ R_S $ between $ V_{DD} $ and the source of M₁. However, for a standard **nMOS common-source amplifier**, $ R_S $ is typically connected **between the source and ground** (not $ V_{DD} $). Assuming this correction (a common convention), the analysis proceeds as follows:
> - **$ V_{DD} \rightarrow R_D \rightarrow \text{Drain} \rightarrow \text{Source} \rightarrow R_S \rightarrow \text{Ground} $**
> - **Gate** is driven by $ V_{in} $.
> - **Output** ($ V_{out} $) is taken at the drain (node between $ R_D $ and M₁).

---

---

## **🔹 2. DC Analysis (Biasing)**
### **Assumptions**
- MOSFET operates in **saturation (active) region** (for amplification).
- Square-law model:  
  $$
  I_D = \frac{1}{2} \mu_n C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} (V_{GS} - V_{th})^2 = \frac{1}{2} k_n (V_{GS} - V_{th})^2
  $$
  where $ k_n = \mu_n C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} $, $ V_{th} $ = threshold voltage.

### **Key Equations**
1. **Source Voltage**:  
   $$
   V_S = I_D R_S
   $$
2. **Gate-Source Voltage**:  
   $$
   V_{GS} = V_{in} - V_S = V_{in} - I_D R_S
   $$
3. **Drain Voltage (Output)**:  
   $$
   V_{out} = V_{DD} - I_D R_D
   $$
4. **Drain-Source Voltage**:  
   $$
   V_{DS} = V_{out} - V_S = V_{DD} - I_D (R_D + R_S)
   $$

### **Saturation Condition**
For the MOSFET to be in saturation:
$$
V_{DS} \geq V_{GS} - V_{th}
$$
Substituting:
$$
V_{DD} - I_D (R_D + R_S) \geq (V_{in} - I_D R_S) - V_{th}
$$
This inequality must hold for proper operation.

### **Solving for $ I_D $**
From $ V_{GS} = V_{in} - I_D R_S $ and the square-law model:
$$
I_D = \frac{1}{2} k_n (V_{in} - I_D R_S - V_{th})^2
$$
This is a **quadratic equation** in $ I_D $. Solving it requires substituting known values of $ V_{in}, V_{th}, k_n, R_S $.

---

---

## **🔹 3. Small-Signal Analysis**
### **Small-Signal Model**
- The MOSFET is replaced by its **hybrid-π model**:
  - Transconductance: $ g_m = \sqrt{2 k_n I_D} $
  - Output resistance: $ r_o = \frac{1}{\lambda I_D} $ (if channel-length modulation is considered, $ \lambda > 0 $).

- **Source degeneration** introduces feedback, reducing gain but improving linearity and stability.

### **Voltage Gain ($ A_v $)**
Using the small-signal equivalent:
$$
A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = -\frac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S}
$$
- **Interpretation**:
  - Without $ R_S $ ($ R_S = 0 $), gain = $ -g_m R_D $ (standard common-source).
  - With $ R_S $, gain is **reduced** due to negative feedback.
  - The negative sign indicates **inversion** (output is 180° out of phase with input).

### **Input Resistance ($ R_{in} $)**
- The gate of a MOSFET has **very high input resistance** (insulated gate).
- Thus, $ R_{in} \approx \infty $ (ideal for voltage amplifiers).

### **Output Resistance ($ R_{out} $)**
- $ R_{out} = R_D \parallel r_o $
- If $ r_o \gg R_D $, then $ R_{out} \approx R_D $.

---

---

## **🔹 4. Key Observations & Applications**
| **Parameter**       | **Value**                          | **Implication** |
|----------------------|------------------------------------|-----------------|
| **Voltage Gain**     | $ A_v = -\frac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S} $ | Lower than standard common-source; more stable. |
| **Input Resistance** | $ R_{in} \approx \infty $        | Ideal for high-impedance inputs. |
| **Output Resistance**| $ R_{out} \approx R_D $            | Depends on $ R_D $ and $ r_o $. |
| **Bias Stability**   | Improved with $ R_S $             | Less sensitive to device variations. |
| **Frequency Response** | Bandwidth limited by $ R_S C_{gs} $ | $ R_S $ introduces a pole at $ f_p = \frac{1}{2\pi R_S C_{gs}} $. |

### **Advantages of Source Degeneration**
- **Linearizes the transfer characteristic** (reduces distortion).
- **Increases input resistance** (though already high for MOSFETs).
- **Stabilizes the bias point** against parameter variations (e.g., $ V_{th} $, $ k_n $).

### **Disadvantages**
- **Reduced gain** compared to a non-degenerated common-source amplifier.
- **Higher output impedance** (if $ R_S $ is large).

---

---

## **🔹 5. Example Calculation (Illustrative)**
Assume:
- $ V_{DD} = 5 \, \text{V} $
- $ R_D = 10 \, \text{k}\Omega $
- $ R_S = 1 \, \text{k}\Omega $
- $ V_{in} = 2 \, \text{V} $
- $ V_{th} = 1 \, \text{V} $
- $ k_n = 1 \, \text{mA/V}^2 $

### **Step 1: Solve for $ I_D $**
From $ V_{GS} = V_{in} - I_D R_S $ and $ I_D = \frac{1}{2} k_n (V_{GS} - V_{th})^2 $:
$$
I_D = \frac{1}{2} (2 - I_D \cdot 1 - 1)^2 = \frac{1}{2} (1 - I_D)^2
$$
Multiply both sides by 2:
$$
2I_D = (1 - I_D)^2 = 1 - 2I_D + I_D^2
$$
Rearrange:
$$
I_D^2 - 4I_D + 1 = 0
$$
Solutions:
$$
I_D = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16 - 4}}{2} = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{12}}{2} = 2 \pm \sqrt{3}
$$
Take the smaller root (since $ I_D $ must be < $ \frac{V_{DD}}{R_D + R_S} = \frac{5}{11} \approx 0.45 \, \text{mA} $):
$$
I_D \approx 2 - 1.732 = 0.268 \, \text{mA}
$$

### **Step 2: Compute $ g_m $**
$$
g_m = \sqrt{2 k_n I_D} = \sqrt{2 \cdot 1 \cdot 0.268} \approx 0.732 \, \text{mS}
$$

### **Step 3: Voltage Gain**
$$
A_v = -\frac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S} = -\frac{0.732 \cdot 10}{1 + 0.732 \cdot 1} \approx -\frac{7.32}{1.732} \approx -4.23
$$

---

---

## **🔹 6. Summary**
| **Aspect**           | **Result** |
|-----------------------|------------|
| **Configuration**     | Common-source with source degeneration |
| **DC Bias**          | Determined by $ V_{in}, V_{th}, R_S, R_D $ |
| **Small-Signal Gain**| $ A_v = -\frac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S} $ |
| **Input Resistance** | $ \approx \infty $ |
| **Output Resistance**| $ R_D \parallel r_o $ |
| **Stability**        | Improved due to $ R_S $ |
| **Phase**            | Inverting (180° phase shift) |

This circuit is widely used in **analog IC design** for its **stability, linearity, and high input impedance**. The trade-off is **reduced gain**, which is acceptable in many applications where precision and stability are critical.

### **Circuit Analysis: PMOS Common-Source Amplifier with Source Degeneration**

---

## **🔹 Circuit Identification**
The given circuit is a **PMOS Common-Source Amplifier with Source Degeneration**, configured as follows:
- **Transistor**: $ M_1 $ (PMOS, as the arrow on the source points *inward* in standard notation).
- **Power Supply**: $ V_{DD} $ (positive voltage rail).
- **Source Resistor**: $ R_S $ (connected between $ V_{DD} $ and the source of $ M_1 $).
- **Drain Resistor**: $ R_D $ (connected between the drain of $ M_1 $ and ground).
- **Input**: $ V_{in} $ (applied to the gate of $ M_1 $).
- **Output**: $ V_{out} $ (taken from the drain node, between $ R_D $ and $ M_1 $).

---

---

## **🔹 DC Operating Point Analysis**
### **Key Assumptions**
- The transistor $ M_1 $ is in **saturation** (typical for amplifiers).
- For a **PMOS**, saturation requires:
  $$
  V_{SD} \geq V_{SG} - |V_{th,p}|,
  $$
  where $ V_{th,p} < 0 $ is the threshold voltage (e.g., $ V_{th,p} = -0.7 \, \text{V} $).

### **DC Equations**
1. **Drain Current ($ I_D $)**:
   - Current flows from $ V_{DD} \rightarrow R_S \rightarrow M_1 \rightarrow R_D \rightarrow \text{GND} $.
   - Let $ V_S $ = source voltage, $ V_D $ = drain voltage.
   - From Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL):
     $$
     V_S = V_{DD} - I_D R_S, \quad V_D = I_D R_D.
     $$
   - Gate-source voltage:
     $$
     V_{GS} = V_{in} - V_S = V_{in} - (V_{DD} - I_D R_S).
     $$
   - For **PMOS in saturation**, the drain current is:
     $$
     I_D = \frac{1}{2} \mu_p C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} (V_{SG} - |V_{th,p}|)^2 (1 + \lambda V_{SD}),
     $$
     where:
     - $ V_{SG} = V_S - V_{in} = V_{DD} - I_D R_S - V_{in} $,
     - $ V_{SD} = V_S - V_D = V_{DD} - I_D (R_S + R_D) $.

2. **Solving for $ I_D $**:
   - Substitute $ V_{SG} $ and $ V_{SD} $ into the saturation equation.
   - This is a **nonlinear equation** in $ I_D $, typically solved numerically or graphically (e.g., using load-line analysis).
   - **Simplified Case (Ignoring Channel-Length Modulation, $ \lambda = 0 $)**:
     $$
     I_D = \frac{1}{2} \mu_p C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} \left( (V_{DD} - V_{in} - I_D R_S) - |V_{th,p}| \right)^2.
     $$
   - The solution depends on $ V_{in} $, $ V_{DD} $, $ R_S $, $ R_D $, and transistor parameters.

---

---

## **🔹 Small-Signal (AC) Analysis**
### **Small-Signal Model**
- **AC Grounds**: $ V_{DD} $ and GND are AC grounds.
- **Transistor Parameters**:
  - Transconductance: $ g_m = \sqrt{2 \mu_p C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} I_D} $,
  - Output resistance: $ r_o = \frac{1}{\lambda I_D} $ (if channel-length modulation is considered).
- **Source Degeneration**: $ R_S $ introduces **negative feedback**, reducing gain but improving linearity and input impedance.

### **Voltage Gain ($ A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} $)**
Using the **T-model** for the MOSFET with source degeneration:
1. **Small-Signal Voltages**:
   - $ v_{gs} = v_{in} - v_s $,
   - $ v_s = -i_d R_S $ (since $ i_d $ flows through $ R_S $ to AC ground),
   - $ v_{out} = -i_d R_D $ (drain voltage across $ R_D $).

2. **Drain Current**:
   $$
   i_d = g_m v_{gs} + \frac{v_{ds}}{r_o} \approx g_m v_{gs} \quad (\text{if } r_o \gg R_D).
   $$

3. **Substitute $ v_{gs} $ and $ v_{out} $**:
   $$
   v_{gs} = v_{in} - (-i_d R_S) = v_{in} + i_d R_S.
   $$
   $$
   i_d = g_m (v_{in} + i_d R_S).
   $$
   Solving for $ i_d $:
   $$
   i_d = \frac{g_m v_{in}}{1 - g_m R_S}.
   $$
   **Note**: The negative sign in the denominator arises from the PMOS configuration (current direction). For **NMOS**, the gain would be $ -\frac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S} $, but for **PMOS**, the sign flips due to the inverted current flow.

4. **Voltage Gain**:
   $$
   A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = \frac{-i_d R_D}{v_{in}} = \frac{-g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S}.
   $$
   - **Key Insight**: The gain is **reduced** by the factor $ (1 + g_m R_S) $ due to source degeneration. This trade-off improves linearity and input impedance.

### **Input Resistance ($ R_{in} $)**
- The gate of a MOSFET has **negligible current** (infinite input resistance in ideal case).
- With source degeneration, the input resistance remains **very high** (typically $ > 10^{12} \, \Omega $) because the gate is isolated by the oxide layer.

### **Output Resistance ($ R_{out} $)**
- Seen from the drain:
  $$
  R_{out} = R_D \parallel r_o.
  $$
  - If $ r_o \gg R_D $, then $ R_{out} \approx R_D $.

---

---

## **🔹 Key Characteristics**
| **Parameter**       | **Expression**                          | **Interpretation**                                                                 |
|----------------------|-----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Voltage Gain**     | $ A_v \approx -\frac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S} $ | Reduced by $ R_S $ (source degeneration stabilizes gain).                        |
| **Input Resistance** | $ R_{in} \approx \infty $             | MOSFET gate has negligible leakage current.                                       |
| **Output Resistance**| $ R_{out} \approx R_D \parallel r_o $  | Dominated by $ R_D $ if $ r_o $ is large.                                         |
| **Saturation Condition** | $ V_{SD} \geq V_{SG} - |V_{th,p}| $ | Ensures $ M_1 $ operates in saturation for amplification.                        |
| **DC Biasing**       | Depends on $ V_{in} $, $ R_S $, $ R_D $ | Sets $ I_D $ and $ V_{GS} $; critical for linear operation.                      |

---

---

## **🔹 Practical Implications**
1. **Source Degeneration ($ R_S $)**:
   - **Pros**: Improves linearity, stabilizes gain against process variations, increases input impedance.
   - **Cons**: Reduces voltage gain (trade-off between gain and stability).

2. **PMOS vs. NMOS**:
   - PMOS is used here because the source is connected to $ V_{DD} $ (positive rail). For NMOS, the source would typically connect to ground.
   - PMOS requires $ V_{GS} < V_{th,p} $ (negative) to turn on, so $ V_{in} $ must be **lower than $ V_S $** for conduction.

3. **Biasing**:
   - To set a stable operating point, $ V_{in} $ must be chosen such that $ M_1 $ is in saturation. For example:
     - If $ V_{DD} = 5 \, \text{V} $, $ R_S = 10 \, \text{k}\Omega $, $ R_D = 20 \, \text{k}\Omega $, and $ V_{th,p} = -1 \, \text{V} $, then $ V_{in} $ must be $ < V_{DD} - |V_{th,p}| $ (e.g., $ V_{in} = 3 \, \text{V} $) to ensure $ V_{SG} > |V_{th,p}| $.

4. **Frequency Response**:
   - Limited by parasitic capacitances (e.g., $ C_{GS} $, $ C_{GD} $) and $ R_S $, $ R_D $. Higher $ R_S $ or $ R_D $ reduces the bandwidth.

---

---

## **🔹 Summary**
- **Circuit Type**: PMOS Common-Source Amplifier with **Source Degeneration**.
- **Function**: Voltage amplification with improved linearity and stability.
- **Gain**: $ A_v \approx -\frac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S} $ (reduced by $ R_S $).
- **Input/Output Impedances**: $ R_{in} \approx \infty $, $ R_{out} \approx R_D $.
- **Key Trade-off**: Source degeneration ($ R_S $) reduces gain but enhances robustness.

> **💡 Note**: For **NMOS-based designs**, the source would connect to ground, and $ V_{DD} $ would be the drain supply. This circuit uses PMOS due to the source connection to $ V_{DD} $. Always verify transistor type via the symbol (arrow direction) and biasing.

$$V_{SD}=V_{S}-V_{D}=V_{DD}-I_{D}(R_{S}+R_{D}) $$

> Cut off: $V_{SG}< |V_{Tp}|$, $I_{D}=0$, $V_{out}=0$.

> Saturation, square law to fix ideas :

$$I_{D}={\frac{1}{2}}k_{p}{\frac{W}{L}}(V_{SG}-|V_{Tp}|)^{2}(1+\lambda V_{SD})$$

$$ {\rm saturation}\;\;V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{Tp}|$$

i. e.

$$V_{S}-V_{D} \ge V_{S}-V_{G}-|V_{Tp}|$$

at the operating point $Q$ with $I_{DQ}$.

-{\frac{1}{2}}V_{SD}^{2}\right]$$

For $V_{G}\to -\infty $, $r_{on}\to 0$

$$V_{out,max}\approx V_{DD}{\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}+R_{D}+r_{on}}}

The DC voltage transfer is therefore inverting, $0$ for

For small signal about $Q$ put $VDD=0$ $AC$.

the current in $R_{D}$ is the transistor current.

KCL $s$: $v_{s}/R_{S}+i_{sd}=0$ so $i_{sd}=-v_{s}/R_{S}$
KCL $d$: $i_{sd}=v_{out}/R_{D}$ for the circuit as drawn,
with no external test source.

Hence for the closed circuit

$$-{\frac{v_{s}}{R_{S}}}= {\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}}=i_{sd} \tag{3}$$

$$v_{s}=-i_{sd}R_{S}\qquad v_{out}=i_{sd}R_{D}$$

From (2)(3)

$${\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}}=g_{m}(v_{s}-v_{in})+g_{mb}v_{sb}+
{\frac{v_{s}-v_{out}}{r_{o}}}$$

Put $v_{s}=-v_{out}R_{S}/R_{D}$ :

$${\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}}= -g_{m}v_{in}
+v_{s}(g_{m}+g_{mb})+{\frac{v_{s}-v_{out}}{r_{o}}}$$

$${\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}}= -g_{m}v_{in}
-{\frac{v_{out}R_{S}}{R_{D}}}(g_{m}+g_{mb})
-{\frac{v_{out}(R_{S}/R_{D}+1)}{r_{o}}}$$

$$v_{out}\left[{\frac{1}{R_{D}}}+{\frac{R_{S}}{R_{D}}}

$$\;A_{v}={\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}}=-
{\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+R_{S}(g_{m}+g_{mb})+(R_{S}+R_{D})/r_{o}}}\;

Special cases:

* $b$ tied to $s$, drawn arrow on source, $v_{sb}=0$, $g_{mb}=0$:

* $r_{o}\to\infty $:

\;\xrightarrow{g_{mb}=0}\;-{\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}}}\tag{5}$$

* $g_{m}R_{S}\gg 1$:

$$A_{v}\to -{\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}}}{\frac{g_{m}}{g_{m}+g_{mb}}}
\to -{\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}}}$$

determined by the resistor ratio. This is series
feedback: $R_{S}$ senses $i_{d}$ and feeds back a voltage
$v_{s}=-i_{d}R_{S}$ in series with $v_{sg}$, linearising
the stage.

Effective transconductance

$$G_{m}={\frac{i_{d}}{v_{in}}}= {\frac{g_{m}}{1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}}}$$

so $A_{v}=-G_{m}R_{D}$.

{\it Input impedance:} Gate oxide

$$Z_{in}=\infty \;\;{\rm low\;frequency},\;\;
C_{in}=C_{gs}+(1-G_{m}R_{D})C_{gd}\;\;{\rm Miller}$$

{\it Output impedance:} Zero $v_{in}$, $v_{g}=0$, apply $v_{x}$

With $R_{D}$ removed, from $v_{s}/R_{S}+g_{m}v_{s}+g_{mb}v_{sb}+
(v_{s}-v_{x})/r_{o}=0$

$$R_{d}\equiv {\frac{v_{x}}{i_{x}}}\Bigl|_{R_{D}\to\infty}
 =r_{o}+R_{S}\left[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o}\right]\tag{6}$$

$g_{mb}=0$ if $b=s$. For $r_{o}\to\infty$, $R_{d}\to\infty$,
ideal current source. 

For the complete stage

$$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel R_{d}
 =R_{D}\parallel\left\{r_{o}+[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o}]R_{S}\right\}
 \approx R_{D}\;\;{\rm if}\;r_{o}{\rm \;large}\tag{7}$$

If $r_{o}$ large the pole at the output is
$\omega_{p}\approx 1/R_{out}C_{L}$, $C_{L}=C_{db}+C_{gd}+C_{load}$.

In words: common source with source degeneration.
$R_{S}$ provides local series-series negative feedback.
It lowers the voltage gain from $-g_{m}R_{D}$ to
$-g_{m}R_{D}/(1+g_{m}R_{S})$, raises the impedance looking
into the drain by $\approx g_{m}r_{o}R_{S}$, improves
linearity, extends bandwidth, and makes the gain less
sensitive to $g_{m}$, approaching $-R_{D}/R_{S}$, at the
expense of headroom $I_{DQ}(R_{S}+R_{D})$ and gain. Up to

answer.text:
That is a $p$ channel ${\rm MOS}$
{\it common source} with {\it un bypassed source
resistance} $R_{S}$ and resistive load $R_{D}$
to $AC$ ground. $+V_{DD}$ is $AC$ ground.

For the symbol drawn bulk $=S$, i. e. $V_{SB}=0$,
$\gamma =0$. If the $n$ well is returned to $V_{DD}$,
$g_{mb}\ne 0$ and

$$V_{T}=V_{T0}+\gamma \left[\sqrt{2\phi _{F}+V_{SB}}-
\sqrt{2\phi _{F}}\right],\qquad V_{SB}=V_{S}-V_{DD}>0\;{\rm dc}$$

and $g_{mb}= \gamma g_{m}/2\sqrt{2\phi _{F}+V_{SB}}$ has
to be carried along.

Put $V_{thp}<0$, $|V_{T}|=-V_{T}$ for the $p$.
$$|I_{D}| = I_{S}=I_{D}$$

in the conventional positive direction $S\to D\to R_{D}\to 0$.

$$\eqalign{
V_{S}&=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S} \cr
V_{D}&=V_{o}=I_{D}R_{D} \cr
V_{SG}&=V_{S}-V_{G}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S}-V_{I} \cr
V_{SD}&=V_{S}-V_{D}=V_{DD}-I_{D}(R_{S}+R_{D})}$$

{\it D.C. large signal:}

* {\bf Cut off:} $V_{SG}<|V_{T}|$

$$I_{D}=0\;\;,\;\;V_{o}=0$$
$$V_{SG}=V_{DD}-V_{I}<|V_{T}|\;:\;V_{I}>V_{DD}-|V_{T}|$$

upto $R_{S}$ drop at the edge.

* {\bf Saturation :} $|V_{SD}|\ge |V_{SG}|-|V_{T}|$,
i. e.

$$V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{T}|$$

$$V_{S}-V_{D}\ge V_{S}-V_{G}-|V_{T}|$$
$$V_{D}\le V_{G}+|V_{T}|\;:\;V_{o}\le V_{I}+|V_{T}|$$

$$|I_{D}| =\tfrac12 \mu_{p}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}
\left(V_{SG}-|V_{T}|\right)^{2}\left(1+\lambda V_{SD}\right)
\tag{1}$$

with $V_{SG}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S}-V_{I}$. Eq.(1) is
quadratic in $I_{D}$ for $\lambda =0$.

$$V_{DD}-V_{I}=|V_{T}|+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{D}}{\mu_{p}C_{ox}W/L}}
+I_{D}R_{S}$$

* {\bf Triode:} $V_{SD}<V_{SG}-|V_{T}|$, $V_{o}>
V_{I}+|V_{T}|$

$$|I_{D}| =\mu_{p}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}\left[
\left(V_{SG}-|V_{T}|\right)V_{SD}-\tfrac12 V_{SD}^{2}\right]
\left(1+\lambda V_{SD}\right)$$

In normal bias $V_{o}$ is in saturation,
$V_{o}<V_{I}+|V_{T}|$. As $V_{I}$ is lowered
$V_{SG}$ grows, $I_{D}$ grows, $V_{o}=I_{D}R_{D}$
rises and the device is driven towards triode
for large $I_{D}R_{D}$.

The useful $VTC$ is inverter like, $V_{o}\approx 0$
for $V_{I}$ high, rising with slope $<0$ when the
device turns on, compressed by the $I_{D}R_{S}$ drop.

$$P_{DC}=V_{DD}I_{D}$$

$$g_{m}= \left.\frac{\partial I_{D}}{\partial V_{SG}}
\right|_{Q}= \mu_{p}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}
\left(V_{SG}-|V_{T}|\right)\left(1+\lambda V_{SD}\right)
\approx \sqrt{2\mu_{p}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}I_{D}}$$

$$r_{o}=1/g_{ds}=1/\lambda I_{D}$$

{\it Small signal $AC$:}

$V_{DD}=0$ AC. Gate $v_{i}$, source $v_{s}$,
drain $v_{o}$.

$$v_{sg}=v_{s}-v_{i}\qquad v_{sd}=v_{s}-v_{o}\qquad
v_{sb}=v_{s}-v_{b}$$

$$i_{d}=g_{m}v_{sg}+g_{mb}v_{sb}+g_{ds}v_{sd}$$

For the symbol $v_{b}=v_{s}\;,\;g_{mb}=0$.
For well to $V_{DD}$, $v_{b}=0$, $v_{sb}=v_{s}$.

$$v_{s}= -i_{d}R_{S}\tag{2}$$
$$v_{o}= i_{d}R_{D}\tag{3}$$

$R_{D}$ to $AC$ ground, $R_{S}$ to $AC$ ground.
So $R_{S}$ is source degeneration, $R_{D}$ is the load.

From (2)-(3):

$$i_{d}=g_{m}(v_{s}-v_{i})+g_{mb}v_{s}+g_{ds}(v_{s}-v_{o})$$

$$i_{d}= -\left(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}\right)i_{d}R_{S}
-g_{m}v_{i}-g_{ds}i_{d}R_{D}$$

$$i_{d}\left[ 1+\left(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}\right)R_{S}+g_{ds}R_{D}
\right]=-g_{m}v_{i}$$

> $$A_{v}\equiv \frac{v_{o}}{v_{i}}=
> -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}+g_{ds}(R_{S}+R_{D})}\tag{4}$$

For bulk $=S$, $g_{mb}=0$:

> $$A_{v}= -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}+(R_{S}+R_{D})/r_{o}}
> =-\frac{g_{m}r_{o}R_{D}}{r_{o}+R_{S}+R_{D}+g_{m}r_{o}R_{S}}$$

In the usual $r_{o}\gg R_{S},R_{D}$:

> $$A_{v}\approx -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}}
> =-\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}+1/g_{m}} \tag{5}$$

Inverting amplifier. Without degeneration $R_{S}=0$:

$$A_{v0}=-g_{m}(R_{D}\parallel r_{o})\approx -g_{m}R_{D}$$

for $r_{o}\to\infty$.

Strong degeneration $g_{m}R_{S}\gg 1$:

$$A_{v}\approx -R_{D}/R_{S}$$

set by resistance ratio, linearised by negative
series feedback. $R_{S}$ stabilises $Q$
point at the price of gain, improves linearity,
reduces distortion and increases bandwidth.

Including $r_{o}$ the more common form of (5) is

$$A_{v}= -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}}\;
\frac{1}{1+\dfrac{R_{S}+R_{D}}{r_{o}(1+g_{m}R_{S})}}$$

{\it Terminal resistances, low frequency:}

$$R_{in}=R_{G}\approx \infty \;{\rm for\;MOS\;gate}$$

$$Z_{in}(s)=1/sC_{g}\;\;{\rm at\;high\;frequency}$$

Looking into the drain with $v_{i}=0$:

$$R_{d}=r_{o}+\left[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o}\right]R_{S}
\approx r_{o}\left[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}\right]$$

Source degeneration boosts the impedance seen at the
drain by $\approx g_{m}R_{S}$.

At the output node

> $$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel R_{d}
> =R_{D}\parallel \left\{r_{o}+[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o}]R_{S}\right\}
> \approx R_{D}\;\;{\rm if}\;R_{D}\ll R_{d} \tag{6}$$

If $R_{D}\gg r_{o}$, $R_{out}\approx R_{d}$.

With a capacitive load $C_{L}$ the dominant pole is

$$\omega_{p o}\approx 1/R_{out}C_{L}\qquad
  \omega_{p s}\approx \frac{1+g_{m}R_{S}}{R_{S}C_{s}}$$

where $C_{s}$ is the capacitance at the source node.
The un-bypassed $R_{S}$ gives a zero/pole doublet.

If $R_{S}$ is bypassed by $C_{S}$, $R_{S}$ disappears
for $ \omega \gg 1/R_{S}C_{S}$ and $A_{v}\to -g_{m}
(R_{D}\parallel r_{o})$.

In short: single-stage, inverting, $g_{m}R_{D}$ class
amplifier with series feedback $R_{S}$. Voltage gain
negative, magnitude $ \sim g_{m}R_{D}/(1+g_{m}R_{S})$,
current gain $\approx 0$, power gain $\approx |A_{v}|$,
high $R_{in}$, $R_{out}\approx R_{D}$, good for
level shifting, resistive load driver, with the
usual $PMOS$ $\approx 2$--$3\times$ lower $g_{m}$ than
$NMOS$ for same size.

answer.text:
This is a ${\rm P}$ channel, common
source with series feedback $:R_{S}$ i.e.
source degenerated ${\rm C.S.}$ with resistive
load. $V_{DD} = AC$ ground.

$$M_{1} : {\rm S\;top,\;D\;bottom,\;G}=V_{in}$$

$${\rm S}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S}\qquad D\equiv V_{out}=I_{D}R_{D}$$
$${\rm S-D\;\;voltage\;\;} V_{SD}=V_{S}-V_{out}=V_{DD}
-I_{D}\left(R_{S}+R_{D}\right)$$

$${\rm S-G\;\;voltage\;\;} V_{SG}=V_{S}-V_{in}
=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S}-V_{in}$$

> If $R_{S}=0$ it is the conventional resistively loaded
> ${\rm C.S.}$ inverter/amplifier with
> voltage gain $-g_{m}R_{D}\parallel r_{o}$ and
> $180^{0}$ phase shift. $R_{S}$ is series-series
> feedback.

\subsection*{1. DC - large signal}

With normal polarities $V_{th,p}<0$, $|V_{th,p}|=-V_{th,p}$

* {\it Cut off} $V_{SG}<|V_{th,p}|$

$$V_{in}>V_{S}-|V_{th,p}| \approx V_{DD}-|V_{th,p}|$$
$$I_{D}=0\;\;,\;\;V_{out}=0$$

* {\it Saturation} $V_{SG}>|V_{th,p}| ,\;V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{th,p}|$

$$I_{D}=k_{p}(V_{SG}-|V_{th,p}|)^{2}\left(1+\lambda_{p}V_{SD}\right)$$
$$k_{p}=\frac12\mu_{p}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}$$

so with $\lambda =0$:

$$I_{D}=k_{p}\left(V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S}-V_{in}-|V_{th,p}|\right)^{2}\tag{1}$$

$$V_{out}=I_{D}R_{D} \tag{2}$$

(1) is quadratic in $I_{D}$. It is made more linear
and less $k_{p}$ sensitive by the $I_{D}R_{S}$ term.

Saturation is maintained for

$$V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{th,p}|$$
$$V_{DD}-I_{D}(R_{S}+R_{D})\ge V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S}-V_{in}-|V_{th,p}|$$
$$V_{in}\ge I_{D}R_{D}-|V_{th,p}| =V_{out}-|V_{th,p}|$$

* {\it Triode} $V_{SD}<V_{SG}-|V_{th,p}|$

$$I_{D}=2k_{p}\left[(V_{SG}-|V_{th,p}|)V_{SD}-\tfrac12V_{SD}^{2}\right]$$

For very low $V_{in}$ the device is a small
$r_{on}=1/[2k_{p}(V_{SG}-|V_{th,p}|)]$ to $V_{DD}$

$$I_{D}\approx \frac{V_{DD}}{R_{S}+R_{D}+r_{on}}\;\;,\;\;
V_{out}\approx V_{DD}\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}+R_{D}+r_{on}} \rightarrow
V_{DD}\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}+R_{D}}$$

So the large signal $V_{out}-V_{in}$ is $0$
for $V_{in}$ high, rising $\propto (V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{th}|)^{2}$
in saturation and flattening in triode.

$$V_{out}\approx R_{D}k_{p}\left(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{th,p}|\right)^{2}
\;{\rm for}\;g_{m}R_{S}\ll 1$$

and with degeneration much more linear.

Headroom cost: $I_{D}R_{S}$ is lost from the available
$V_{SD}$ swing.

\subsection*{2. Small signal}

Gate $Z_{in}= \infty $ at low frequency, $C_{gs},C_{gd}$
at high frequency.

$$g_{m}= \left.\frac{\partial I_{D}}{\partial V_{SG}}\right|
_{Q}=2\sqrt{k_{p}I_{DQ}}= \frac{2I_{DQ}}{V_{SGQ}-|V_{th}|}$$
$$r_{o}=1/\lambda_{p}I_{DQ}\;\;,\;\;g_{mb}= \eta g_{m}$$
$\eta \approx 0.1-0.3$ if body to $V_{DD}$, $0$ if
body tied to ${\rm S}$.

AC ground $V_{DD}=0$. 

$$\begin{aligned}
v_{sg} &= v_{s}-v_{in} \\
v_{sd} &= v_{s}-v_{out} \\
i_{d} &= g_{m}v_{sg}+g_{mb}v_{sb}+ \frac{v_{sd}}{r_{o}} 
\end{aligned}$$

With body to $V_{DD}$, $v_{sb}=v_{s}-0=v_{s}$.
With body to ${\rm S}$, $g_{mb}=0$.

Resistor constraints AC:

$$v_{s}= -i_{d}R_{S}\qquad v_{out}= i_{d}R_{D}$$

Hence

$$i_{d}= g_{m}(v_{s}-v_{in})+g_{mb}v_{s}+ \frac{v_{s}-v_{out}}{r_{o}}$$
$$i_{d}\left[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}+\frac{R_{S}}{r_{o}}\right]
+\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o}}=-g_{m}v_{in}$$

With $v_{out}=i_{d}R_{D}$:

$$A_{v}\equiv \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
-\frac{g_{m}R_{D}r_{o}}{r_{o}\left[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}\right]
+R_{S}+R_{D}} \tag{3}$$

$${\rm Commonly\; }A_{v}= -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}
{1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}+ \dfrac{R_{S}+R_{D}}{r_{o}}}$$

* Body to source: $g_{mb}=0$

$$A_{v}= -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}+ (R_{S}+R_{D})/r_{o}}$$

* $r_{o}\rightarrow \infty $:

$$A_{v}\approx -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}}
\approx -\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}}\;\;{\rm for}\;\;g_{m}R_{S}\gg 1$$

* No degeneration $R_{S}\rightarrow 0$:

$$A_{v0}= -g_{m}\left(R_{D}\parallel r_{o}\right)
\approx -g_{m}R_{D}$$

inverting. $R_{S}$ trades gain for:

* linearisation, reduction of distortion $\propto 1/(1+g_{m}R_{S})$
* desensitisation to $g_{m},\,k_{p}$
* larger input linear range $\Delta V_{in}\approx I_{D}R_{S}$
* higher output resistance and bandwidth $f_{-3dB}\approx 1/R_{out}C_{L}$

The source degeneration can be by-passed with $C_{S}$ for
AC: $R_{S}(AC)=R_{S}\parallel 1/sC_{S}$ so DC stability
is kept and AC gain $A_{v0}$ is recovered for $f\gg 1/R_{S}C_{S}$.

$$Z_{in}=1/sC_{g}\rightarrow \infty \;{\rm LF}$$

Looking into the drain with $v_{in}=0$ the impedance
seen is the well known common gate with source resistance:

$$R_{d}= r_{o}+\left[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o}\right]R_{S}
\approx \left[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}\right]r_{o}$$

At the output node

$$R_{out}= R_{D}\parallel R_{d}= R_{D}\parallel
\left\{r_{o}+[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o}]R_{S}\right\} $$

$$\approx R_{D}\parallel [1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}]r_{o}$$

For $R_{S}=0$, $R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel r_{o}$.

Similarly impedance looking into the source with drain
load $R_{D}$ is $\approx (R_{D}+r_{o})/(1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o})$.

At high frequency $C_{gs},C_{gd},C_{db},C_{sb}$ create
a dominant pole at the output $\omega_{p1}\approx 1/R_{out}C_{L}$
and a pole/zero at the source $\omega_{p2}\approx (1+g_{m}R_{S})/R_{S}C_{s}$.

In feedback terms $R_{S}$ samples the current and feeds
back a voltage $i_{d}R_{S}$ in series with $v_{in}$.

> Bias $I_{D}$ chosen to give required $g_{m}$, swing
> $I_{D}R_{D}<V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S}-V_{DSsat}$ and power
> $P=V_{DD}I_{D}$.

If you give $W/L,\;V_{DD},\;R_{S},R_{D},\;V_{th},\;k_{p},\;\lambda$
(3) can be evaluated numerically. E.g. $g_{m}=1\,{\rm mS}$,
$R_{D}=5\,{\rm k\Omega }$, $R_{S}=0.5\,{\rm k\Omega }$,
$r_{o}\gg R_{D}$: $A_{v0}\approx -5$, $A_{v}\approx
-5/(1+0.5)=-3.3$.

answer.text:
This is a pMOS common-source stage with
source degeneration.

* $M_{1}$ is pMOS. The upper terminal is the source,
the lower is the drain. The n-well - the arrow -
is strapped to the source so $V_{SB}=0$.
* Source is to $V_{DD}$ through $R_{S}$,
drain is to ground through $R_{D}$.
* Gate is the input, drain is the output.

For a.c. $V_{DD}$ is ground. The source sees
$R_{S}$ to ground, the drain sees $R_{D}$ to ground.
It is topologically identical to the nMOS CS
with $R_{S}$ to ground, $R_{D}$ to $V_{DD}$.

Qualitatively it is inverting. Increase $V_{G}$,
$V_{SG}$ falls, $I_{D}$ falls, $I_{D}R_{D}$
falls.

### D.C. bias

Let for $M_{1}$ in saturation

$$I_{D}=\frac12 \mu_{p}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}
\left(V_{SG}-|V_{THP}|\right)^{2}
\left(1+\lambda_{p}V_{SD}\right)$$

With the polarities in the figure:

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{S} &= V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S} \\
V_{D} &= I_{D}R_{D}=V_{out,DC} \\
V_{G} &= V_{in,DC} \\
V_{SG} &= V_{S}-V_{G}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S}-V_{G} \\
V_{SD} &= V_{S}-V_{D}=V_{DD}-I_{D}(R_{S}+R_{D})
\end{aligned}$$

ON: $V_{SG}>|V_{THP}|$

Saturation for pMOS:

$$V_{SD} \ge V_{SG}-|V_{THP}|$$

i.e.

$$V_{D} \le V_{G}+|V_{THP}|$$

If OFF, $I_{D}=0$, $V_{out}=0$, $V_{S}=V_{DD}$.
If $V_{G}$ is very low $I_{D}$ rises,
$V_{S}$ falls, $V_{D}$ rises and the device
goes triode.

Small signal:

$$g_{m} = \frac{\partial I_{D}}{\partial V_{SG}},\qquad
r_{o}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{p}I_{D}}$$

$$g_{m}\approx \sqrt{2\mu_{p}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}I_{D}}$$

No back gate; body is tied to source.

### Small-signal voltage gain

$\pi$-model: gate $v_{g}=v_{in}$, source $v_{s}$,
drain $v_{d}=v_{out}$. $R_{S}$ from source to
ac ground, $R_{D}$ from drain to ac ground.
Between drain-source: $g_{m}v_{gs}$ from drain
to source in parallel with $r_{o}$, with
$v_{gs}=v_{g}-v_{s}$.

KCL source:

$$\frac{v_{s}}{R_{S}}-g_{m}v_{gs}-\frac{v_{d}-v_{s}}{r_{o}}=0$$

KCL drain:

$$\frac{v_{d}}{R_{D}}+g_{m}v_{gs}+\frac{v_{d}-v_{s}}{r_{o}}=0$$

with $v_{gs}=v_{in}-v_{s}$.

Adding, the transistor current cancels:

$$\frac{v_{s}}{R_{S}}+\frac{v_{d}}{R_{D}}=0$$

i.e. all a.c. source current goes through $R_{D}$,
as must be since gate draws no current.

Eliminating $v_{s}=-(R_{S}/R_{D})v_{d}$:

$$\frac{v_{d}}{R_{D}}+g_{m}v_{in}
+g_{m}\frac{R_{S}}{R_{D}}v_{d}
+\frac{1+R_{S}/R_{D}}{r_{o}}v_{d}=0$$

Hence

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
-\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}+\dfrac{R_{S}+R_{D}}{r_{o}}}$$

This is the classic CS with degeneration.

If $r_{o}\gg R_{S},R_{D}$:

$$A_{v}\approx -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}}
= -\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}+1/g_{m}}$$

$R_{S}$ degenerates. For $R_{S}=0$,
$A_{v}=-g_{m}(R_{D}\parallel r_{o})$.

The stage inverts, $180^{\circ}$ phase.

### Input and output resistance

Gate draws no low-frequency current:

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

For $R_{out}$, set $v_{in}=0$, apply $v_{x}$
at the drain. Let $i_{x}'$ be the current into
the drain, exclusive of $R_{D}$. Then
$v_{s}=i_{x}'R_{S}$, $v_{gs}=-v_{s}$,

$$i_{x}' = g_{m}v_{gs}+\frac{v_{x}-v_{s}}{r_{o}}
= -g_{m}R_{S}i_{x}'+\frac{v_{x}-R_{S}i_{x}'}{r_{o}}$$

$$\frac{v_{x}}{i_{x}'}=r_{o}+(1+g_{m}r_{o})R_{S}$$

In parallel with $R_{D}$ to ground:

$$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel\left[r_{o}+(1+g_{m}r_{o})R_{S}\right]$$

Typically the bracket is $\gg R_{D}$, so

$$R_{out}\approx R_{D}$$

$R_{S}$ raises the impedance looking into the
drain by bootstrapping, at the price of gain
reduction, but improves linearity and bias
stability.

This is a PMOS common source stage.

* top is the source: $R_{S}$ to $V_{DD}$ ac ground
* bottom is the drain: $R_{D}$ to GND ac ground
* gate is the input, drain is the output

DC current must flow down from $V_{DD}$ to GND
through $R_{S}-M_{1}-R_{D}$. That is possible with
source on top only for PMOS.

Let for DC

$$V_{S}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S}$$
$$V_{D}=I_{D}R_{D}=V_{out}$$
$$V_{G}=V_{in,DC}$$
$$V_{SG}=V_{S}-V_{G}$$
$$V_{SD}=V_{S}-V_{D}=V_{DD}-I_{D}(R_{S}+R_{D})$$

In saturation

$$I_{D}=\frac12 \mu_{p}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}
(V_{SG}-|V_{THP}|)^{2}(1+\lambda_{p}V_{SD})$$

On: $V_{SG}>|V_{THP}|$
Saturated: $V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{THP}|$

i.e.

$$I_{D}R_{D}=V_{out}\le V_{G,DC}+|V_{THP}|$$

$V_{out}=0$ for $M_{1}$ off. Up $M_{1}$ goes to triode.

Small signal it is exactly the same as an NMOS
CS with source degeneration. $V_{DD}$ is ac ground.

As $V_{in}\uparrow$, $V_{SG}\downarrow$,
$I_{SD}\downarrow$, drop on $R_{D}\downarrow$,
$V_{out}\downarrow$. Inverting.

Let $v_{g}=v_{in}$, $v_{s}$ = source ac,
$v_{d}=v_{out}$ = drain ac,

$$v_{sg}=v_{s}-v_{g}$$
$$v_{sd}=v_{s}-v_{d}$$
$$v_{sb}=v_{s}-v_{b}$$

Transistor source to drain ac current:

$$i_{sd}=g_{m}v_{sg}+g_{mb}v_{sb}+g_{ds}v_{sd}$$

$g_{ds}=1/r_{o}$.

KCL source: $R_{S}$ to ground:

$$ \frac{v_{s}}{R_{S}}+i_{sd}=0 $$

KCL drain: $R_{D}$ to ground:

$$i_{sd}=\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}$$

Hence

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}=
g_{m}(v_{s}-v_{in})+g_{mb}(v_{s}-v_{b})
+g_{ds}(v_{s}-v_{out})$$

with $v_{s}=-(R_{S}/R_{D})v_{out}$.

If the n-well is tied to the source, $v_{b}=v_{s}$,
$v_{sb}=0$, no back gate:

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}=-g_{m}v_{in}
-\left(g_{m}+g_{ds}\right)\frac{R_{S}}{R_{D}}v_{out}
-g_{ds}v_{out}$$

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
= \frac{-g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}+g_{ds}(R_{S}+R_{D})}$$

$$A_{v}= \frac{-g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}+(R_{S}+R_{D})/r_{o}}$$

This is the classic

$$A_{v}=-G_{m}(R_{D}\parallel r_{o}')$$

with effective transconductance reduced by
series feedback:

For $r_{o}\to\infty$:

$$A_{v}\approx \frac{-g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}}$$

If $g_{m}R_{S}\gg 1$:

$$A_{v}\approx -\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}}$$

$R_{S}$ is source degeneration: it trades gain
for linearity, reduces $G_{m}$ to $g_{m}/(1+g_{m}R_{S})$.

If body is tied to $V_{DD}$ ac ground, $v_{b}=0$,
$v_{sb}=v_{s}$, replace $g_{m}R_{S}$ by
$(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}$:

$$A_{v}= \frac{-g_{m}R_{D}}
{1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}+(R_{S}+R_{D})/r_{o}}$$

Input resistance at low frequency:

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

gate draws no current.

Output resistance: put $v_{in}=0$, apply $v_{x}$
at output. Looking into the drain:

$$R_{d}=R_{S}+r_{o}+(g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o}R_{S}$$
$$=r_{o}[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}]+R_{S}$$

In parallel with $R_{D}$:

$$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel R_{d}$$

With body to source $g_{mb}=0$:

$$R_{d}=r_{o}(1+g_{m}R_{S})+R_{S}$$

Usually $R_{d}\gg R_{D}$, so

$$R_{out}\approx R_{D}$$

Source degeneration boosts the impedance looking
into the drain by $\approx 1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})R_{S}$
but it is still shunted by $R_{D}$.

answer.text:
This is a PMOS common-source stage.

Top is higher DC than bottom, so for a PMOS the
top is the source, the bottom is the drain.
$R_{S}$ to $V_{DD}$ ac ground is a source
degeneration resistor, $R_{D}$ to ground is the
drain load. Output is taken at the drain.
Input is to the gate.

The 3-terminal symbol has body tied to source,
so $V_{BS}=0$, no back-gate effect.

Put $V_{DD}$ ac ground. AC wise source sees
$R_{S}$ to gnd, drain sees $R_{D}$ to gnd,
exactly like a NMOS CS with $R_{S}$ degeneration.

### Large signal

Let source be S top, drain D bottom.

$$V_{S}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S}$$
$$V_{D}=I_{D}R_{D}=V_{out}$$
$$V_{SG}=V_{S}-V_{G}$$
$$V_{SD}=V_{S}-V_{D}=V_{DD}-I_{D}(R_{S}+R_{D})$$

In saturation:

$$I_{D}=\frac12 \mu_{p}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}
(V_{SG}-|V_{THP}|)^{2}(1+\lambda_{p}V_{SD})$$

Saturation for PMOS:

$$V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{THP}|$$

i.e.

$$V_{D}\le V_{G}+|V_{THP}|$$

Operation: $V_{in}$ high near $V_{DD}$: $V_{SG}<|V_{THP}|$,
$M_{1}$ off, $I_{D}=0$, $V_{S}=V_{DD}$, $V_{out}=0$.

Decrease $V_{in}$ so $V_{DD}-V_{in}>|V_{THP}|$:
$M_{1}$ turns on, $I_{D}>0$, $V_{out}=I_{D}R_{D}$
rises, $V_{S}$ falls. This is the amplifying
quadratic region.

For large $I_{D}$, $V_{SD}=V_{DD}-I_{D}(R_{S}+R_{D})$
falls and $M_{1}$ enters triode. This limits
the maximum $V_{out}$.

It is an inverting amplifier.

### Small signal

Saturation, $g_{m}$, $r_{o}=1/g_{ds}$:

$$g_{m}=\sqrt{2\mu_{p}C_{ox}(W/L)I_{D}}$$

Gate: $v_{g}=v_{in}$, source: $v_{s}$,
drain: $v_{d}=v_{out}$.

$$v_{gs}=v_{g}-v_{s}$$
$$v_{ds}=v_{d}-v_{s}$$

Current into drain:

$$i_{d}=g_{m}v_{gs}+g_{ds}v_{ds}$$

KCL source: $R_{S}$ to ac gnd:

$$\frac{v_{s}}{R_{S}}+i_{s}=0$$

$i_{s}=-i_{d}$, so

$$v_{s}=i_{d}R_{S}$$

KCL drain: $R_{D}$ to ac gnd:

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}+i_{d}=0$$

so

$$i_{d}=-\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}$$
$$v_{s}=-\frac{R_{S}}{R_{D}}v_{out}$$

Then

$$i_{d}=g_{m}(v_{in}-v_{s})+g_{ds}(v_{out}-v_{s})$$

$$-\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}=g_{m}v_{in}+g_{ds}v_{out}
-(g_{m}+g_{ds})v_{s}$$

Insert $v_{s}$:

$$-\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}=g_{m}v_{in}+g_{ds}v_{out}
+(g_{m}+g_{ds})\frac{R_{S}}{R_{D}}v_{out}$$

$$v_{out}\left[\frac1{R_{D}}+g_{ds}+
(g_{m}+g_{ds})\frac{R_{S}}{R_{D}}\right]=-g_{m}v_{in}$$

Voltage gain:

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
-\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+(g_{m}+g_{ds})R_{S}+g_{ds}R_{D}}$$

$$A_{v}= -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}
{1+g_{m}R_{S}+(R_{S}+R_{D})/r_{o}}$$

With $r_{o}\to\infty$:

$$A_{v}\approx -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}}
= -\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}+1/g_{m}}$$

$R_{S}$ is series-series negative feedback,
degeneration. It reduces gain, linearizes,
stabilizes. If $g_{m}R_{S}\gg 1$:

$$A_{v}\approx -\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}}$$

resistor ratio.

Input resistance at low frequency, gate draws
no DC current:

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

Output resistance: set $v_{in}=0$, drive
drain with $v_{x}$, measure $i_{x}$.

This gives impedance looking into drain with
$R_{S}$ in source:

$$R_{d}=r_{o}+(1+g_{m}r_{o})R_{S}$$

in parallel with $R_{D}$:

$$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel\left[r_{o}+(1+g_{m}r_{o})R_{S}\right]$$

$$\approx R_{D}\parallel r_{o}(1+g_{m}R_{S})$$

For large $r_{o}$, $R_{out}\approx R_{D}$.
Degeneration boosts the drain impedance.

answer.text:
$M_{1}$ is a PMOS device. Its source is the upper terminal,
tied through $R_{S}$ to $V_{DD}$, its drain is the lower terminal,
tied through $R_{D}$ to ground. The input is applied to the
gate and the output is taken at the drain.

It is therefore a common-source stage with resistive load
$R_{D}$ and with unbypassed source degeneration $R_{S}$.
The body is tied to the source, as shown by the arrow, so
$V_{BS}=0$ and there is no body effect.

### 1. DC bias

Let $I_{D}>0$ denote the current flowing from source to drain.
The same current flows in $R_{S}$ and $R_{D}$.

$$
V_{S}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S},\qquad 
V_{out,Q}=V_{D}=I_{D}R_{D}
$$

$$
V_{SG}=V_{S}-V_{G}=V_{DD}-V_{in,Q}-I_{D}R_{S}
$$
$$
V_{SD}=V_{S}-V_{D}=V_{DD}-I_{D}(R_{S}+R_{D})
$$

In saturation, neglecting $\lambda$ for the bias equation,

$$
I_{D}= \frac{\beta_{p}}{2}\,
\Bigl(V_{SG}-|V_{Tp}|\Bigr)^{2},
\qquad 
\beta_{p}= \mu_{p}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}
$$

i.e.

$$
I_{D}= \frac{\beta_{p}}{2}\,
\Bigl(V_{DD}-V_{in,Q}-I_{D}R_{S}-|V_{Tp}|\Bigr)^{2}.
$$

$R_{S}$ provides DC negative feedback: an increase in $I_{D}$
lowers $V_{S}$ and hence $V_{SG}$, opposing the increase. The
bias point is therefore stabilized.

For saturation we require

$$
V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{Tp}|\equiv V_{OV},
\qquad 
g_{m}= \beta_{p}V_{OV}= \sqrt{2\beta_{p}I_{D}},\qquad 
r_{o}= \frac{1}{\lambda_{p}I_{D}} .
$$

When $V_{in}$ is raised toward $V_{DD}$, $V_{SG}$ decreases,
$M_{1}$ turns off, $I_{D}\to0$ and $V_{out}\to0$. When $V_{in}$
is lowered, $I_{D}$ and $V_{out}$ increase until $M_{1}$ enters
the triode region. The stage is inverting.

### 2. Small-signal voltage gain

Use the small-signal model with $g_{m}$ referred to $v_{sg}$.
$V_{DD}$ and ground are both ac ground. Let $i_{d}$ be the
small-signal source-to-drain current. Then

$$
v_{out}=i_{d}R_{D},\qquad v_{s}=-i_{d}R_{S}
$$

the minus sign in $v_{s}$ being because an increase in the
current through $R_{S}$ increases the drop from $V_{DD}$.

Also

$$
i_{d}=g_{m}v_{sg}+\frac{v_{sd}}{r_{o}}
     =g_{m}(v_{s}-v_{in})+\frac{v_{s}-v_{out}}{r_{o}} .
$$

Substituting $v_{s}$ and $v_{out}$,

$$
i_{d}= -g_{m}v_{in}
       -g_{m}R_{S}i_{d}
       -\frac{R_{S}+R_{D}}{r_{o}}i_{d},
$$

$$
i_{d}= -\,\frac{g_{m}}
{1+g_{m}R_{S}+ \dfrac{R_{S}+R_{D}}{r_{o}}}\,v_{in}.
$$

Hence

$$
\,A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
      =-\,\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}
      {1+g_{m}R_{S}+ \dfrac{R_{S}+R_{D}}{r_{o}}}\, 
$$

or equivalently

$$
A_{v}= -\,\frac{g_{m}r_{o}R_{D}}
{r_{o}+R_{D}+R_{S}\bigl(1+g_{m}r_{o}\bigr)} .
$$

For $r_{o}\gg R_{S},R_{D}$,

$$
A_{v}\approx -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}}
          =-\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}+1/g_{m}} .
$$

If also $g_{m}R_{S}\gg1$,

$$
A_{v}\approx -\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}},
$$

set by a resistor ratio, largely independent of $g_{m}$.
Degeneration thus reduces gain but improves linearity,
gain stability and bandwidth. For $R_{S}=0$ this reduces to
the familiar $A_{v}=-g_{m}(R_{D}\parallel r_{o})$.

### 3. Input and output resistance

Input resistance: the gate draws no (low-frequency) current,

$$
R_{in}= \frac{v_{in}}{i_{in}} \approx \infty .
$$

Output resistance: with $v_{in}=0$, the resistance looking
into the drain is boosted by source degeneration,

$$
R_{\text{drain}} = r_{o}+R_{S}+g_{m}r_{o}R_{S}
                 = R_{S}+ \bigl(1+g_{m}R_{S}\bigr)r_{o}.
$$

At the output terminal this is in parallel with $R_{D}$:

$$
\,R_{out}=R_{D}\;\Big\|\;
\Bigl[R_{S}+\bigl(1+g_{m}R_{S}\bigr)r_{o}\Bigr]\approx R_{D}\,
$$

in most practical cases, since $R_{D}$ is usually much
smaller than the boosted drain resistance.

In summary: a PMOS inverting common-source amplifier,
whose gain magnitude is reduced from $g_{m}R_{D}$ by the
local series feedback factor $1+g_{m}R_{S}$, with essentially
infinite input resistance and output resistance approximately
$R_{D}$.

answer.text:
The transistor is a PMOS device. The terminal with the arrow
is the source, on top, the other channel terminal is the drain,
at the bottom. The body is tied to the source.

$$V_{DD}\to R_{S}\to S\;{\rm of}\;M_{1}\;,\qquad 
D\;{\rm of}\;M_{1}\to R_{D}\to {\rm GND}$$

$V_{in}$ is on the gate, $V_{out}$ is on the drain. It is a
common-source stage, with a resistor $R_{S}$ in the source
lead - source degeneration - and a resistive load $R_{D}$ in
the drain. The body-source junction is shorted, $V_{BS}=0$,
so there is no body effect.

### 1. D.C. operation

Let $I_{D}$ be the current flowing from source to drain.
The same current flows in $R_{S}$ and $R_{D}$.

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{S} &= V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S} \\
V_{out}=V_{D} &= I_{D}R_{D} \\
V_{SG} &= V_{S}-V_{in}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S}-V_{in}\\
V_{SD} &= V_{S}-V_{D}=V_{DD}-I_{D}(R_{S}+R_{D})
\end{aligned}$$

$V_{in}$ must supply the d.c. gate bias. $M_{1}$ is off for

$$V_{SG}<|V_{Tp}|\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; V_{in}>V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|$$

in which case $I_{D}=0$ and $V_{out}=0$. 

For $M_{1}$ in saturation, $\lambda\approx 0$,

$$ I_{D}=\frac{\beta_{p}}{2}\big(V_{SG}-|V_{Tp}|\big)^{2},
\qquad \beta_{p}= \mu_{p}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L} $$

i.e. with $\Delta = V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{Tp}|$

$$ I_{D}= \frac{\beta_{p}}{2}\big(\Delta-I_{D}R_{S}\big)^{2} $$

$$I_{D}= \frac{\;\beta_{p}R_{S}\Delta+1-\sqrt{1+2\beta_{p}R_{S}\Delta}\;}
{\beta_{p}R_{S}^{2}}\;\;{\rm in\;saturation}$$

Saturation requires $V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{Tp}|$, i.e.

$$V_{D}\le V_{G}+|V_{Tp}|\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
I_{D}R_{D}\le V_{in,DC}+|V_{Tp}| .$$

Increasing $V_{in}$ decreases $V_{SG}$, decreases $I_{D}$ and
hence decreases $V_{out}=I_{D}R_{D}$: the stage is inverting.
For very low $V_{in}$ $M_{1}$ enters triode and $V_{out}$ tends
to the resistive divider $V_{DD}R_{D}/(R_{S}+R_{D}+r_{on})$.

### 2. Small-signal voltage gain

$V_{DD}$ is a.c. ground. $R_{S}$ is between source and a.c.
ground, $R_{D}$ between drain and ground. With $v_{sg}=v_{s}-v_{in}$,

$$i_{d}=g_{m}v_{sg}+\frac{v_{s}-v_{out}}{r_{o}},\qquad 
i_{d}= \frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}},\qquad v_{s}=-i_{d}R_{S}$$

whence

$$\,A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
      =-\,\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}
                {\,1+g_{m}R_{S}+\dfrac{R_{S}+R_{D}}{r_{o}}}\,  $$

$$A_{v}= -\frac{g_{m}r_{o}R_{D}}{R_{D}+r_{o}+R_{S}+g_{m}r_{o}R_{S}} $$

For $r_{o}\gg R_{S},R_{D}$

$$A_{v}\approx -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}} $$

the familiar degenerated common-source gain. The effective
transconductance is $g_{m}/(1+g_{m}R_{S})$.

If $g_{m}R_{S}\gg1$,

$$A_{v}\approx -\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}}$$

i.e. the gain is set by a resistor ratio, much less sensitive
to $g_{m}$, $V_{T}$ and temperature, and much more linear,
at the expense of $|A_{v}|$ and of headroom $I_{D}R_{S}$.
$R_{S}$ is local series-series feedback: a rise in $v_{in}$
tends to lower $i_{d}$, lowering $v_{s}$ drop and opposing the change in $v_{sg}$.

With an external load, replace $R_{D}$ by $R_{D}\parallel R_{L}$.

### 3. Input and output resistance

Gate input, at low frequency,

$$R_{in}\approx \infty$$

apart from $C_{gs},C_{gd}$ at high frequency.

Looking into the drain, source degeneration boosts the
resistance to 

$$R_{out,M}=R_{S}+r_{o}+g_{m}r_{o}R_{S}
          =r_{o}(1+g_{m}R_{S})+R_{S}$$

so that at the output terminal

$$\,R_{out}=R_{D}\;\Big\|\;\big[\,r_{o}(1+g_{m}R_{S})+R_{S}\,\big]\,$$

usually $\approx R_{D}$ if $R_{D}$ is not very large.

In summary: a PMOS inverting common-source amplifier with
source degeneration. Gain is $-g_{m}R_{D}/(1+g_{m}R_{S})$ to
first order, input resistance is very high, output resistance is
essentially $R_{D}$, and $R_{S}$ trades gain for linearity,
predictability and bias stability.
