answer.text:
$M_{1}$ is a p-channel device. The terminal with the arrow
is the source, the body is tied to the source, and the lower
terminal is the drain. The body-source junction is therefore
at zero bias in the signal sense.

$$V_{B}=V_{S}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad g_{mb}=0$$

$V_{DD}$ is a signal ground. This is a common-source stage
with an unbypassed resistance $R_{S}$ in the source, i.e. local
series feedback, and a resistive load $R_{D}$ in the drain.
The signal is applied to the gate and taken from the drain,
so the stage is inverting.

### 1. Bias

Let $I_{D}$ be the current flowing from source to drain.
The same current flows in $R_{S}$ and $R_{D}$.

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{S} &= V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S} \\
V_{out,Q}=V_{D} &= I_{D}R_{D} \\
V_{SG} &= V_{S}-V_{in,Q}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{S}-V_{in,Q}\\
V_{SD} &= V_{S}-V_{D}=V_{DD}-I_{D}(R_{S}+R_{D})
\end{aligned}$$

The device is off for $V_{SG}<|V_{Tp}|$, i.e. for
$V_{in}\gtrsim V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|$, in which case $I_{D}=0$ and
$V_{out}=0$.

In saturation, neglecting channel length modulation,

$$ I_{D}= \frac{\beta_{p}}{2}
\bigl(V_{SG}-|V_{Tp}|\bigr)^{2},
\qquad 
\beta_{p}= \mu_{p}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L} $$

i.e.

$$ I_{D}= \frac{\beta_{p}}{2}
\Bigl[V_{DD}-V_{in,Q}-|V_{Tp}|-I_{D}R_{S}\Bigr]^{2} \tag{1} $$

$R_{S}$ makes (1) implicit in $I_{D}$: an increase in $I_{D}$
raises the drop in $R_{S}$, lowers $V_{SG}$ and opposes the
increase. The $Q$-point is therefore stabilised against
$V_{Tp}$ and $\beta_{p}$ variations, at the cost of headroom
$I_{D}R_{S}$ at the source.

Saturation requires $V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{Tp}|$, i.e.

$$ V_{D}\le V_{G}+|V_{Tp}|
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
V_{out}\le V_{in}+|V_{Tp}| $$

If $V_{in}$ is made too negative $I_{D}$ and $V_{out}=I_{D}R_{D}$
rise until this is violated and $M_{1}$ enters the triode
region.

At the $Q$-point

$$g_{m}= \beta_{p}\bigl(V_{SG}-|V_{Tp}|\bigr)=\sqrt{2\beta_{p}I_{D}},
\qquad 
r_{o}= \frac{1}{\lambda_{p} I_{D}} $$

### 2. Small-signal gain

With $v_{dd}=0$, let $i_{d}$ be the signal source-to-drain
current, $v_{s}$ the signal source voltage and $v_{out}$ the
signal drain voltage. KCL at source and drain gives

$$v_{s}=-i_{d}R_{S}, \qquad v_{out}=i_{d}R_{D}$$

and for the transistor, with no body effect,

$$i_{d}=g_{m}v_{sg}+\frac{v_{sd}}{r_{o}}
      =g_{m}(v_{s}-v_{in})+\frac{v_{s}-v_{out}}{r_{o}} .$$

Substituting $v_{s}$ and $v_{out}$,

$$i_{d}= -g_{m}v_{in}
-\left[g_{m}R_{S}+\frac{R_{S}+R_{D}}{r_{o}}\right]i_{d}$$

so that the effective transconductance from gate to drain is

$$G_{m,eff}\equiv\frac{i_{d}}{v_{in}}
= -\,\frac{g_{m}}
{1+g_{m}R_{S}+(R_{S}+R_{D})/r_{o}}$$

and

$$\,A_{v}\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
= -\,\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}
{1+g_{m}R_{S}+(R_{S}+R_{D})/r_{o}}
= -\,\frac{g_{m}r_{o}R_{D}}
{r_{o}+R_{S}+R_{D}+g_{m}r_{o}R_{S}}\, \tag{2}$$

The minus sign is the usual common-source phase inversion:
$v_{in}\uparrow \Rightarrow V_{SG}\downarrow \Rightarrow
I_{D}\downarrow \Rightarrow V_{out}=I_{D}R_{D}\downarrow$.

For $r_{o}\gg R_{S},R_{D}$, (2) reduces to the familiar
degenerated form

$$A_{v}\approx -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+g_{m}R_{S}}
= -\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}+1/g_{m}}$$

and for $g_{m}R_{S}\gg1$,

$$A_{v}\approx -\frac{R_{D}}{R_{S}} $$

i.e. the gain is set by a resistor ratio, is largely
independent of $g_{m}$, and is much more linear than an
undegenerated CS stage. Degeneration trades gain for
linearity, predictability and bandwidth.

If an external load $R_{L}$ is present, replace $R_{D}$ by
$R_{D}\parallel R_{L}$ in the numerator of (2).

### 3. Input and output resistance

The gate draws no (low-frequency) current:

$$R_{in}= \infty$$

in parallel, at high frequency, with $C_{gs}$ and the
Miller-multiplied $C_{gd}$. Because $|A_{v}|$ is reduced
by degeneration, the Miller effect is also reduced.

The resistance looking into the drain of a source-degenerated
device is raised by the feedback:

$$R_{drain}= r_{o}+R_{S}+g_{m}r_{o}R_{S}
= R_{S}+ \bigl(1+g_{m}R_{S}\bigr)r_{o}$$

Hence at the output node

$$\,R_{out}= R_{D}\,\Big\|\,
\Bigl[R_{S}+ \bigl(1+g_{m}R_{S}\bigr)r_{o}\Bigr]\,$$

usually $R_{out}\approx R_{D}$ since the bracketed term is
$\gg R_{D}$.

In summary: a PMOS common-source amplifier with source
degeneration $R_{S}$ and drain load $R_{D}$, no body effect,
gain $\approx -R_{D}/(R_{S}+1/g_{m})$, infinite input resistance,
and output resistance essentially $R_{D}$.

Circuit identification  
The transistor symbol shows the source at the top and the drain at the bottom; the arrow on the bulk points from the ­channel toward the source, i.e. it is a p-channel MOSFET (PMOS).  
The dc supply is therefore “up-side-down”:  

VDD → RS → source (S) – M1 – drain (D) → RD → GND  

ID flows from VDD down to ground through the series path RS – M1 – RD.  
The gate is driven by the input Vin (referred to ground).  
The drain node is the output Vout.  
This is the p-channel counterpart of the familiar common–source amplifier, but with a source–degeneration resistor RS that provides local feedback.

-------------------------------------------------
1. Large-signal (bias) equations
-------------------------------------------------
Assume the transistor operates in saturation (|VSD| ≥ |VSG| – |VTP|) and neglect λ first.

ID = ½ βp (W/L) (VSG – |VTP|)^2   βp≡μpCox

with  VSG = VS – VG = (VDD – IDRS) – Vin

Therefore

ID = ½ βp (W/L) (VDD – IDRS − Vin − |VTP|)^2    (1)

(1) is a quadratic equation in √ID that can be solved numerically, or graphically as the intersection of the device i–v curve and the straight line IDRS = VDD − Vin − |VTP| − VSG.

When channel-length modulation is included (λ ≠ 0),

ID = ½ βp (VSG – |VTP|)^2 (1 + λVSD)  with VSD = VS – VD = (VDD – IDRS) − Vout

-------------------------------------------------
2. Conditions for proper operation
-------------------------------------------------
• Conduction (device on):
 VSG ≥ |VTP| ⇒ Vin ≤ VDD − IDRS − |VTP|

• Saturation:
 VSD ≥ VSG − |VTP| ⇒ Vout ≥ Vin + |VTP|

• Voltage head-room:
 0 V ≤ Vout ≤ VDD − IDRS   (lower limit is set by RD, upper by the drop across RS)

These inequalities give the usable Vin range and show how RS makes the bias point self-adjusting: if ID tends to rise, the larger drop IDRS reduces VSG and pushes the current back down.

-------------------------------------------------
3. Small-signal model
-------------------------------------------------
Small-signal schematic (ac grounds are shown as ↓):

                ↑ (ac ground) VDD  
                         RS  
                         │  
     vin ───CG──→|        ◄──── gm·vgs , ro  
                 │                     │  
                 └───vs (≠0)           │  
                         │            vo = –id(RD ∥ ro')  
                         │  
                        RD  
                         ↓ ground

ro’ is ro referred from drain to source (≈ro if VS is an ac ground).

Relations:

vs = id RS                            vgs = vin − vs  
id = gm vgs         ⇒ id = gm (vin − idRS) = gm vin / (1 + gmRS)

-------------------------------------------------
4. Small-signal gain, input & output resistances
-------------------------------------------------
Voltage gain (ro ≫ RD, RS for simplicity):

Av = vout / vin = – id RD / vin  
   = – gm RD / (1 + gm RS)                 (2)

• Without degeneration (RS = 0) → Av = – gm RD (ordinary PMOS CS stage)  
• With RS ≫ 1/gm         → Av ≈ – RD / RS (feedback-dominated, nearly β-independent)

Input resistance Rin: gate of a MOS device ≈ ∞ (limited only by gate oxide leakage or the bias network).

Output resistance Rout (at the drain):

If ro is included, Rout ≈ (RD ∥ ro) (1 + gm RS)   
(the 1+gmRS term represents the familiar “local-feedback boosting” of the output resistance).

-------------------------------------------------
5. What the source resistor does
-------------------------------------------------
1. Stabilises the quiescent current and operating point against:
   • Process variation (β, VTP)  
   • Temperature  
   • Supply changes (ΔVDD)

   Sensitivity: ∂ID/∂Vin = gm /(1+gmRS), ∂ID/∂|VTP| = –gm /(1+gmRS)

2. Improves linearity (reduces gain variation with signal).

3. Trades gain and voltage swing for the above benefits and consumes extra head-room (IDRS).

-------------------------------------------------
6. Design procedure (example roadmap)
-------------------------------------------------
Given VDD, desired ID, gain |Av|, RD and device β:

a. Pick RS from (2): RS = (gm RD − |Av|)/(|Av| gm)  
   where gm = √(2βID) (saturation).

b. Check head-room: VDD ≥ IDRS + |VTP| + required VSDsat + largest |Vin|.

c. Verify saturation: Vout(min) (≈0 V at full swing) must satisfy Vout ≥ Vin(max) + |VTP|.

d. Re-iterate including λ if better accuracy is needed.

-------------------------------------------------
Key take-aways
• The circuit is a source-degenerated PMOS common-source amplifier.  
• Source resistor RS introduces local (series) feedback that lowers gain but makes the bias point and gain far more robust.  
• Small-signal gain: Av = – gmRD / (1 + gmRS).  
• Very high input impedance (MOS gate).  
• Output impedance is roughly (RD ∥ ro)(1 + gmRS).  
• Proper bias requires VSG ≥ |VTP| and VSD ≥ VSG − |VTP|; RS reduces the available voltage swing by the drop IDRS.

3. DC (large–signal) analysis

        where        VSG = VS – VG      , VSD = VS – Vout
        Saturation requires VSD ≥ VSG – |VTP|.

   b) Ohm’s law for the two resistors

        ID = ( VDD – VS ) / RS                          (2)
        ID = Vout / RD                                  (3)

   c) Combining (2) and (3)

        Vout = ( RD / RS ) ( VDD – VS )                 (4)

   d) Insert VS from (2) in (1) (or vice-versa) to obtain an implicit

    a. Regions of operation  

       The controlling quantity for a PMOS device is VSG = VS – VG (all voltages measured with respect to ground).

       • Cut–off: VSG < |VT|  
         (or VS – VG < |VT|).  
         In this region ID = 0 ⇒ VS = VDD,  VD = 0 ⇒ VOUT = 0.

       • Saturation: VSG ≥ |VT|  and  VSD > VSG – |VT|  
         The channel equation (neglecting λ) is  
         ID = ½ kP (VSG – |VT|)^2,  kP = μpCox(W/L).

       • Triode: VSG ≥ |VT|  and  VSD ≤ VSG – |VT|  
         ID = kP[(VSG – |VT|)VSD – ½ VSD²].

    b. Bias (saturation assumed — the normal small-signal operating region)

         ID = ½ kP(VSG – |VT|)²  
         = ½ kP(VDD – IDRS – VG – |VT|)²        (because VS = VDD – IDRS)

         For a given VIN(=VG) this is a cubic equation in ID that can be solved numerically or graphically; once ID is known

              VS  = VDD – IDRS
              VOUT(=VD) = IDRD.

         The circuit therefore behaves as a self-biased inverter:  
         • VIN high (≈VDD) → M1 cut off → VOUT ≈ 0.  
         • VIN low (near ground) → M1 on → VOUT ≈ IDRD, a positive value that can approach VDD if RD is large.

         The presence of RS automatically sets the drain current and keeps M1 in saturation over a wide VIN range; without RS the bias would be extremely sensitive to device parameters.

3.  Small-signal model  

    With the Mosfet in saturation we use the hybrid-π model (ro may be included if high accuracy is needed).

         gm  = 2ID/(VSG – |VT|) = √(2kPID)          (no λ)  
         rs  = RS                                (external resistor)  
         rd  = RD || ro                          (ro may be large → rd ≈ RD).

    Looking into the gate the resistance is practically infinite, so the incremental source node rises by

         vS = –gm rs · vgs              (negative sign because increasing VG lowers VSG).

    The effective (degenerated) transconductance seen looking into the drain is therefore

         gmeff = gm / (1 + gmRS).

    Small-signal gain (ro neglected for clarity)

         Av = vout / vin
            = – gmeff RD
            = – gm RD / (1 + gm RS).

    Important observations

    • Because of the minus sign the stage is inverting (as in a conventional NMOS common-source amplifier).  
    • RS lowers the magnitude of the gain and at the same time linearises the transfer characteristic and greatly reduces the dependence on the exact value of |VT| or kP.  
    • The input resistance ≃ ∞ (MOS gate), the output resistance ≃ RD (‖ ro if included).

4.  Summary of key equations

    Cut-off limit: VIN > VDD – |VT| ⇒ VOUT ≈ 0.  
    Saturation current: ID = ½ kP (VDD – IDRS – VIN – |VT|)².  
    Output voltage: VOUT = IDRD.  
    Small-signal gain: AV = –gmRD / (1 + gmRS).

    By choosing RS large enough to satisfy gmRS ≫ 1, the circuit can be biased so that AV approaches –RD/RS (a convenient design guideline) and remains quite insensitive to process spreads in kP or |VT|.

## 🧮 DC Bias Analysis (Q-point)

To find the DC operating point (quiescent point), we assume the MOSFET is in **saturation**:

### 1. Gate Voltage:
Since gate is connected to `V_in` (DC bias), we assume `V_G = V_in` (DC component).

### 2. Source Voltage:
`V_S = I_D * R_S`

### 3. Gate-Source Voltage:
`V_GS = V_G - V_S = V_in - I_D * R_S`

### 4. Drain Current (Saturation Region):
For MOSFET in saturation:
```
I_D = (1/2) * k_n * (W/L) * (V_GS - V_th)^2
```
where:
- `k_n` = process transconductance parameter
- `W/L` = aspect ratio
- `V_th` = threshold voltage

Substitute `V_GS`:
```
I_D = (1/2) * k_n * (W/L) * (V_in - I_D * R_S - V_th)^2
```

This is a **quadratic equation in I_D** — solve for `I_D` numerically or graphically.

### 5. Drain Voltage:
`V_D = V_DD - I_D * R_D`

### 6. Output Voltage (DC):
`V_out = V_D = V_DD - I_D * R_D`

We now analyze the **small-signal voltage gain**, **input impedance**, and **output impedance**.

```
A_v = -g_m * R_D / (1 + g_m * R_S)
```

*   **Deriving Voltage Gain ($A_v = v_{\text{out}} / v_{\text{in}}$):**

    The gate voltage is $v_{\text{in}}$.
    The source-gate voltage is $v_{sg} = v_s - v_{\text{in}}$.

    $$ \frac{v_s}{R_S} + g_m(v_s - v_{\text{in}}) = 0 $$
    $$ v_s \left( \frac{1}{R_S} + g_m \right) = g_m v_{\text{in}} $$

## 1. What the circuit is

Reading the symbol and the terminal connections:

* **M₁ is a PMOS transistor.** The bulk/substrate arrow is on the **top** terminal, and that top terminal is the one tied (through $R_S$) to the highest potential ($V_{DD}$). For a PMOS the bulk must sit at the most‑positive terminal, so this is the only consistent reading. (If it were an NMOS the body would have to be the ground‑side terminal, not the $V_{DD}$‑side one.)
* **Source** = top terminal → to $V_{DD}$ through $R_S$.
* **Drain** = bottom terminal → to ground through $R_D$ and to $V_{out}$.
* **Bulk = Source** (the arrow terminal is the same node as the source). Hence $V_{SB}=0$ and **there is no body effect**.
* **Gate** = input $V_{in}$.

So the input is at the gate, the output is at the drain, and the source is returned to AC‑ground ($V_{DD}$) **through** $R_S$. This is a **common‑source (CS) stage with source degeneration $R_S$ and drain load $R_D$** (inverting). Note that $R_S$ and $R_D$ play the "opposite" positions from an NMOS CS stage, which is exactly what you expect for a PMOS (source to the supply, drain to ground).

A second important point: there is **no separate bias network** – the gate is driven directly by $V_{in}$. Therefore $V_{in}$ (its DC level) sets the operating point; the stage is DC‑coupled.

---

## 2. DC analysis (saturation)

Let $I_D$ be the drain current (flows $V_{DD}\to$ source $\to$ drain $\to$ ground). Then

$$V_S = V_{DD} - I_D R_S,\qquad V_D = V_{out} = I_D R_D$$

$$V_{SG} = V_S - V_{in} = V_{DD} - V_{in} - I_D R_S$$

In saturation ($V_{SG}>|V_T|$ and $V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_T|$), with $k_p=\mu_p C_{ox}(W/L)$:

$$I_D = \tfrac{k_p}{2}\big(V_{SG}-|V_T|\big)^2 = \tfrac{k_p}{2}\big(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_T|-I_D R_S\big)^2$$

This quadratic fixes $I_D$ (and hence $V_{out}=I_D R_D$) for a given $V_{in}$. Saturation additionally requires

$$V_{SD}=V_{DD}-I_D(R_S+R_D)\ \ge\ V_{SG}-|V_T|$$

Outside these limits the device is in triode (or cut‑off, if $V_{SG}<|V_T|$).

---

## 3. Small‑signal analysis

Let $v_s, v_d(=v_{out})$ be the small‑signal source and drain node voltages, and $v_{gs}=v_{in}-v_s$. Using the standard MOS small‑signal model ($g_m$ and $r_o$ between D and S), KCL at the source and drain nodes (both $R_S$ and $R_D$ go to AC ground) gives the compact transfer function

$$\boxed{\,A_v = \dfrac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = -\,\dfrac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S + \dfrac{R_S+R_D}{r_o}}\,}$$

* With $r_o\to\infty$: $\;A_v = -\dfrac{g_m R_D}{1+g_m R_S}$ (inverting).
* $R_S=0$: $A_v = -g_m(R_D\parallel r_o)$, the ordinary CS gain.
* **Large degeneration** ($g_m R_S\gg 1$): $A_v \approx -\dfrac{R_D}{R_S}$, i.e. the gain is set by the *resistor ratio*, independent of device parameters, and the effective transconductance is $\approx 1/R_S$.

**Input resistance:** $R_{in}=\infty$ (MOS gate).

**Output resistance** (looking into the drain node with $v_{in}=0$): the degenerated CS output resistance at the drain is $r_o(1+g_m R_S)+R_S$, in parallel with $R_D$:

$$\boxed{\,R_{out} = R_D \,\big\|\, \big[\,r_o(1+g_m R_S)+R_S\,\big]\,}$$

---

## 4. Role of the components / summary

* $R_D$ – drain **load**; sets the output voltage swing and (with $g_m$) the gain.
* $R_S$ – **source degeneration** resistor: provides local (series) negative feedback that (i) reduces and linearises the gain, (ii) stabilises $I_D$ against $k_p$ and $V_T$ variations, and (iii) raises the output resistance. In the deep‑degeneration limit the gain collapses to the passive ratio $-R_D/R_S$.
* $V_{in}$ – provides **both** the signal and the DC gate bias (no bias network present).
* Bulk tied to source ⇒ no body effect; device operates as a clean, inverting, high‑input‑impedance common‑source amplifier with source degeneration.

In short: it is a **DC‑coupled, source‑degenerated PMOS common‑source amplifier**, inverting, with $R_{in}\to\infty$, gain $A_v=-g_mR_D/[1+g_mR_S+(R_S+R_D)/r_o]$, and $R_{out}=R_D\parallel[r_o(1+g_mR_S)+R_S]$.

with $\beta_p=\mu_p C_{ox}W/L$. Defining the overdrive $V_{OV}=V_{SG}-|V_{tp}|=\sqrt{2I_D/\beta_p}$ and $V_0=V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{tp}|$, this becomes the quadratic

$$\frac{R_S}{2\beta_p}V_{OV}^2+V_{OV}-V_0=0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; V_{OV}=\frac{\beta_p}{R_S}\Big(\sqrt{1+\tfrac{2R_S V_0}{\beta_p}}-1\Big),\quad I_D=\frac{V_{OV}^2}{2\beta_p}$$

and $V_{out}=I_D R_D$.

**Conduction / saturation conditions**

* $V_0>0$ (i.e. $V_{DD}-V_{in}>|V_{tp}|$) for the device to turn on.
* Saturation requires $V_{SD}\ge V_{OV}$, i.e. $V_{DD}-I_D(R_S+R_D)\ge V_{OV}$, which also sets the maximum swing of $V_{out}$.

If the body is tied to $V_{DD}$ (the usual reverse‑bias choice for a PMOS whose source sits near $V_{DD}$), then $V_{BS}=V_{DD}-V_S\neq0$ and the body effect must be included; it increases the effective $R_S$ seen by the channel (see §3).

---

## 3. Small‑signal model and gain

AC‑grounds: $V_{DD}$ (top of $R_S$) and ground (bottom of $R_D$). Let $v_s$ and $v_d=v_{out}$ be the small signals at source and drain, and $v_g=v_{in}$. With $g_m$, $g_{mb}$, $r_o$ and $v_{gs}=v_{in}-v_s$, $v_{bs}=-v_s$ (body at AC ground):

$$i_{ds}=g_m v_{gs}+g_{mb}v_{bs}+\frac{v_d-v_s}{r_o}$$

KCL at source and drain ($i_{ds}=v_s/R_S=-v_d/R_D$) gives $v_s=-(R_S/R_D)\,v_d$, and after substitution:

$$\boxed{\,A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=-\,\frac{g_m R_D}{\,1+(g_m+g_{mb})R_S+\dfrac{R_S+R_D}{r_o}\,}\,}$$

* **Ideal** ($r_o\to\infty$, body effect neglected): $\displaystyle A_v=-\frac{g_m R_D}{1+g_m R_S}$ (inverting).
  * If $R_S=0$ this reduces to the familiar $-g_m R_D$.
  * It is useful to read this as $A_v=-G_m R_D$ with the *degenerated* stage transconductance $G_m=\dfrac{g_m}{1+g_m R_S}$ – $R_S$ is local negative feedback that lowers the gain by the factor $1+g_mR_S$.
* **With body effect** (body to $V_{DD}$) the term $g_mR_S$ becomes $(g_m+g_{mb})R_S$, further reducing the gain.

$R_S$ does **not** appear in the numerator, so it only reduces gain; it does not change the sign.

---

## 4. Input and output resistance

* **Input resistance:** $R_{in}=\infty$ (MOS gate; no DC or AC gate current). $R_S$ has no effect on $R_{in}$.
* **Output resistance** (looking into the drain, $v_{in}=0$): applying a test source,

$$\boxed{\,R_{out}=\frac{r_o}{1+R_S(g_m+g_{mb})+R_S/r_o}\;\approx\;r_o\,[1+R_S(g_m+g_{mb})]\,}$$

i.e. source degeneration **boosts the output resistance** (a desirable property for a CS stage, e.g. when used as a high‑impedance amplifier). Neglecting $g_{mb}$, $R_{out}\approx r_o(1+g_mR_S)$.

---

## 5. Summary / role of $R_S$

| Quantity | Expression (ideal) |
|---|---|
| Topology | PMOS common‑source, source degenerated |
| $I_D$ (DC) | from $\frac{R_S}{2\beta_p}V_{OV}^2+V_{OV}-(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{tp}|)=0$ |
| $V_{out}$ (DC) | $I_D R_D$ |
| $A_v$ | $-\dfrac{g_m R_D}{1+g_mR_S}$ |
| $G_m$ (stage) | $\dfrac{g_m}{1+g_mR_S}$ |
| $R_{in}$ | $\infty$ |
| $R_{out}$ | $\approx r_o(1+g_mR_S)$ |

$R_S$ introduces source (local) negative feedback: it **reduces the voltage gain** and makes it **less sensitive to $g_m$ variations**, **improves linearity**, and **increases the output resistance**. The price paid is the lower gain; the input resistance stays infinite. For correct operation $V_{in}$ must provide a DC gate bias that keeps M1 in the saturation region (conditions in §2), and the body should be tied to $V_{DD}$ to keep the body–source junction reverse biased (this adds the $g_{mb}$ terms shown above).

## 1. What the circuit is

Reading the symbol carefully:

* The **gate** of M₁ is driven by $V_{in}$.
* The **arrow (source terminal)** is on the *top* lead, which is tied to $V_{DD}$ through $R_S$.
* The *bottom* lead (drain) is tied to ground through $R_D$, and $V_{out}$ is taken at this bottom node.

Because the source is the **higher‑potential** terminal (it sits near $V_{DD}$), M₁ must be a **PMOS** device. (For an NMOS the source/arrow would be on the bottom, lower‑potential node.)

So the topology is a **common‑source (CS) amplifier, degenerated by $R_S$**, built with a PMOS:

* $V_{DD}$ → **AC ground**
* $R_S$ = source resistor (source → AC ground) – provides DC bias path *and* source degeneration
* $R_D$ = drain load (drain → ground) – the voltage‑converting load
* Input at the gate, output at the drain ⇒ **inverting** stage, very high input impedance.

---

## 2. DC / bias analysis

Let $I_D$ be the (positive) current flowing from $V_{DD}$ through $R_S$, into the source, out of the drain, and through $R_D$ to ground.

$$V_S = V_{DD} - I_D R_S,\qquad V_D = V_{out} = I_D R_D$$
$$V_{SG} = V_S - V_{in} = V_{DD} - V_{in} - I_D R_S$$
$$V_{SD} = V_{DD} - I_D(R_S+R_D)$$

In saturation,

$$I_D = \tfrac{1}{2}\,k_p\frac{W}{L}\,(V_{SG}-|V_{thp}|)^2,\qquad g_m = k_p\frac{W}{L}(V_{SG}-|V_{thp}|)=\frac{2I_D}{V_{SG}-|V_{thp}|}$$

Substituting $V_{SG}$ gives an implicit (quadratic) equation for $I_D$ once the DC level of $V_{in}$ is fixed. **Saturation condition:**

$$V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{thp}|\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad V_{out}=I_D R_D \le V_{in}+|V_{thp}|$$

(plus $V_{SG}\ge |V_{thp}|$ for conduction).

---

## 3. Small‑signal analysis

With $V_{DD}$ and ground shorted, $R_S$ goes from source to AC ground and $R_D$ from drain to AC ground. Using the universal MOSFET small‑signal relation (current *into* the drain) $i_d = g_m v_{gs} + (v_d-v_s)/r_o$, and $v_g=v_{in}$, $v_d=v_{out}$:

* Source node: $\;v_s/R_S = i_d$
* Drain node: $\;v_d/R_D + i_d = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; i_d = -v_d/R_D$

Hence $v_s = -(R_S/R_D)\,v_d$. Substituting into the device equation and solving:

$$\boxed{\,A_v \equiv \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = \frac{-g_m R_D}{\,1 + g_m R_S + \dfrac{R_S+R_D}{r_o}\,}\,}$$

* **With $r_o\to\infty$:** $\;A_v \approx \dfrac{-g_m R_D}{1+g_m R_S}$
* The negative sign confirms the **inverting** (CS) action: raising $V_{in}$ lowers $V_{SG}$, reduces $I_D$, and lowers $V_{out}$.
* $R_S$ is a **degeneration** resistor: it reduces the gain by the factor $1+g_m R_S$, but improves linearity, widens bandwidth, and raises the output resistance.

**Input resistance:** $R_{in}=\infty$ (gate draws no current).

**Output resistance** (looking into $v_{out}$ with $v_{in}=0$):

$$R_{out} = R_D \,\big\|\, \big[\,R_S + r_o + g_m R_S r_o\,\big] \;\approx\; R_D \,\big\|\, \big[r_o(1+g_m R_S)+R_S\big]$$

i.e. much larger than $R_D$ alone because of the degeneration‑boosted look‑in resistance at the drain.

---

## 4. Summary

| Item | Value / observation |
|---|---|
| Device / config | PMOS, **common‑source with source degeneration** |
| AC reference | $V_{DD}$ = AC ground |
| Phase | Inverting ($A_v<0$) |
| Gain | $-g_m R_D/(1+g_m R_S)$ (or the $r_o$‑loaded form above) |
| $R_{in}$ | $\infty$ |
| $R_{out}$ | $R_D\,\|\,[r_o(1+g_m R_S)+R_S]$ |
| Bias | Set by DC $V_{in}$ via $I_D=\frac12 k_p\frac WL(V_{DD}-V_{in}-I_DR_S-|V_{thp}|)^2$; saturation requires $V_{out}\le V_{in}+|V_{thp}|$ |
| Role of $R_S$ | DC source path + negative feedback (lower gain, higher $R_{out}$, better linearity) |
| Role of $R_D$ | Drain load converting $I_D$ into $V_{out}$ |

In short, the figure is the **PMOS mirror image of a standard degenerated NMOS common‑source stage** (where $V_{DD}$ and ground would be swapped), giving an inverting voltage amplifier whose gain is set by $g_m R_D/(1+g_m R_S)$.

A current I_D flows V_DD → R_S → source→drain → R_D → ground:

- V_S = V_DD − I_D·R_S, V_D = I_D·R_D, V_SG = V_DD − I_D·R_S − V_in

- Drain node: i_D + v_out/R_D = 0 ⇒ v_s = −(R_S/R_D)·v_out
- Device: i_D = g_m(v_in − v_s) + (v_out − v_s)/r_o

$$R_{out} = R_D \parallel \big[\,r_o + R_S + (g_m + g_{mb})\,r_o R_S\,\big]$$

- **Inverting:** raising V_in reduces |V_GS| of the PMOS, I_D falls, and v_out = I_D·R_D falls ⇒ negative gain.
- **Limits:** R_S = 0 → simple CS stage, A_v = −g_m(R_D ∥ r_o); R_S ≫ 1/g_m → A_v ≈ −R_D/R_S (gain set by resistor ratio, linearized).

- **Output swing:** v_out can swing from ≈ 0 (device near cutoff) up to the point where M1 leaves saturation (V_out ≈ V_in + |V_TH|).

This is consistent with the resistor labels: R_S sits in the source branch, R_D in the drain branch.
- **Topology:** Input at the gate, output at the drain, source connected to AC ground (V_DD) through R_S ⇒ this is a **common‑source (CS) stage with source degeneration R_S and load resistor R_D**. It is an inverting voltage amplifier.

## DC (bias) relations

The same current I_D flows through R_S, M₁, and R_D:

- V_S = V_DD − I_D·R_S, V_out = V_D = I_D·R_D
- Conduction requires V_SG = V_DD − I_D·R_S − V_in > |V_TH|
- Saturation requires V_SD ≥ V_SG − |V_TH| ⇔ **V_out = I_D·R_D ≤ V_in + |V_TH|**

So R_S sets (together with V_in) the bias current, and R_D sets the output DC level.

## Small‑signal analysis

With v_in at the gate, v_s at the source node, v_d = v_out at the drain node, and including r_o:

- Source node KCL: i = v_s/R_S (i = drain→source device current)
- Drain node KCL: v_out = −i·R_D
- Device: i = g_m(v_in − v_s) + (v_d − v_s)/r_o

Solving:

**Voltage gain**

A_v = v_out/v_in = − g_m·R_D / [ 1 + g_m·R_S + (R_S + R_D)/r_o ]

For r_o → ∞ (ideal transistor):

A_v ≈ − g_m·R_D / (1 + g_m·R_S) = − R_D / (1/g_m + R_S)

**Input resistance:** R_in = ∞ (gate terminal, at low frequency).

**Output resistance:** looking into the degenerated drain gives r_o + R_S + g_m·r_o·R_S, in parallel with R_D:

R_out = R_D ∥ [ r_o + R_S + g_m·r_o·R_S ] ≈ R_D ∥ (g_m·r_o·R_S);  if r_o → ∞, R_out = R_D.

## Interpretation / design comments

- **Inverting amplifier:** the minus sign confirms the CS nature (raising V_in reduces |V_GS| of the PMOS, reducing I_D and raising V_out... equivalently, gain is negative).
- **Role of R_S (degeneration):** it reduces the gain from g_m·R_D to ≈ R_D/(1/g_m + R_S), but makes the gain depend on a resistor ratio (more linear, less sensitive to g_m), and boosts the output resistance seen at the drain. It also consumes headroom (drops I_D·R_S between V_DD and the source).
- **Role of R_D:** converts the drain current to the output voltage; it limits R_out and, together with I_D, sets the output DC level and swing.
- **Limiting cases:** if R_S → 0 (or is bypassed by a large capacitor), A_v → −g_m·R_D (plain CS stage). If g_m·R_S ≫ 1, A_v → −R_D/R_S (resistor-ratio amplifier).

**Summary:** PMOS common-source amplifier with source degeneration R_S and drain load R_D; A_v = −g_m R_D/[1 + g_m R_S + (R_S+R_D)/r_o], R_in = ∞, R_out = R_D ∥ [(1+g_m r_o)R_S + r_o].

The circuit shown is a **Common Source (CS) Amplifier** using a MOSFET. Here is a detailed analysis:

### 1. Circuit Identification
*   **Transistor ($M_1$):** It is a MOSFET. Based on the arrow on the source/body terminal pointing **inwards** towards the channel, it is an **N-channel MOSFET**. (Note: If the arrow were pointing outwards, it would be a P-channel MOSFET. The biasing in the diagram suggests a P-channel configuration for standard operation, but we will analyze it as drawn with an N-channel device).
*   **Configuration:**
    *   **Input ($V_{in}$):** Applied to the Gate.
    *   **Output ($V_{out}$):** Taken from the Drain.
    *   **Common Terminal:** The Source.
    *   This confirms it is a **Common Source Amplifier**.
*   **Resistors:**
    *   **$R_S$:** Source resistor, connected to $V_{DD}$.
    *   **$R_D$:** Drain resistor, connected to Ground.

### 2. DC Biasing Analysis
Assuming $M_1$ is an **N-channel MOSFET** and $V_{DD}$ is a positive supply:
*   For the N-channel MOSFET to conduct, $V_{GS} > V_{th}$.
*   Current ($I_D$) flows from Drain to Source.
*   In this circuit, the Source is connected to $V_{DD}$ via $R_S$, and the Drain is connected to Ground via $R_D$.
*   For current to flow from Drain to Source, it must flow **from Ground, up through $R_D$, into the Drain, through the channel to the Source, and up through $R_S$ to $V_{DD}$**.
*   This requires:
    *   $V_D > V_S$ (since current flows D $\to$ S).
    *   $V_D = I_D R_D$ (Voltage at Drain relative to Ground).
    *   $V_S = V_{DD} - I_D R_S$ (Voltage at Source relative to Ground, since current flows up to $V_{DD}$).
    *   Condition: $I_D R_D > V_{DD} - I_D R_S \Rightarrow I_D(R_D + R_S) > V_{DD}$.
    *   Also, $V_G > V_S + V_{th} \Rightarrow V_{in} > V_{DD} - I_D R_S + V_{th}$.
*   This biasing is possible but requires a relatively high input voltage $V_{in}$ and high drain current $I_D$.

*Alternative Interpretation (P-channel MOSFET):*
*   If $M_1$ is a **P-channel MOSFET** (arrow pointing out), the standard biasing applies:
    *   Current flows from $V_{DD}$, through $R_S$, into the Source, through the channel to the Drain, and down through $R_D$ to Ground.
    *   $V_S \approx V_{DD}$.
    *   $V_D \approx 0$.
    *   $V_{out} = V_D = I_D R_D$.
    *   This is the standard configuration for a P-channel Common Source amplifier.

### 3. Small Signal Analysis (AC Analysis)
Assuming $V_{DD}$ and Ground are AC grounds:
*   **Input Impedance ($R_{in}$):** Very high (ideally infinite), as it is a MOSFET gate.
*   **Output Impedance ($R_{out}$):** Approximately $R_D$ (in parallel with $r_o$ if channel length modulation is considered).

**Case A: N-channel MOSFET (As drawn)**
*   Current leaves the Source (flows up to $V_{DD}$).
*   The source voltage $v_s$ (AC) is negative relative to $V_{DD}$ (AC Ground).
*   $v_{gs} = v_{in} - v_s = v_{in} + |v_s|$.
*   This creates **Positive Feedback**.
*   Voltage Gain ($A_v$):
    $$A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = \frac{g_m R_D}{1 - g_m R_S}$$
*   If $g_m R_S < 1$, the gain is positive (Non-Inverting).
*   If $g_m R_S > 1$, the gain is negative (Inverting) and potentially unstable.

**Case B: P-channel MOSFET (Standard Interpretation)**
*   Current enters the Source (from $V_{DD}$).
*   The source voltage $v_s$ (AC) is negative relative to $V_{DD}$.
*   Wait, for P-channel, $i_d$ (leaving Drain) is negative.
*   $v_{out} = V_D$.
*   $V_D = I_D R_D$ (Current flows down).
*   Gain $A_v$:
    $$A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} \approx - \frac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S}$$
*   This is a standard **Inverting Common Source Amplifier** with Source Degeneration. The resistor $R_S$ provides negative feedback, stabilizing the bias and increasing linearity, but reducing the gain.

### Conclusion
Based on standard circuit design principles, this is likely a **Common Source Amplifier** using a **P-channel MOSFET** (despite the arrow appearing to point in, which might be a drawing artifact or specific symbol style).

### 2. Detailed Analysis
